chapters.n: Luke opens like a careful historian. Many others had already written accounts of what Christians believed about Jesus, setting events in order.

f.g: Undertaken, attempted.
Fully established, firmly accepted.

chapters.n: Those accounts came from people who had been eyewitnesses from the start and who served as ministers of the word. Luke wasn’t an eyewitness himself, so he relied on those who were.

f.g: Servants of the message — those who preached the gospel.

chapters.n: Having researched everything carefully from the beginning, Luke decided to write an orderly account for “most excellent Theophilus” — perhaps a Roman official or a patron.

f.g: Having traced everything accurately.
Greek “friend of God” or “loved by God”; Acts is also addressed to him.

chapters.n: His purpose: so Theophilus could be sure the things he had been taught were true. Luke writes to strengthen faith with solid history.

f.g: Greek katēcheō, taught orally — the root of “catechism.”

chapters.n: The story begins in the reign of Herod the Great with a priest, Zacharias, of the priestly division of Abijah. His wife Elisabeth also descended from Aaron — a doubly priestly family.

f.g: Herod the Great, king of Judea under Rome, who died around 4 BC.
Abijah’s division — one of 24 rotating groups of priests.

chapters.n: Both were righteous in God’s eyes, faithfully keeping all the Lord’s commandments and ordinances.

f.g: Without fault in the eyes of the law — faithful, not sinless.

chapters.n: Yet they had no children, because Elisabeth couldn’t conceive, and both were old. Like Abraham and Sarah, they faced a long sorrow that God would turn into joy.

f.g: Unable to have children — often seen then as a cause of shame.
Advanced in age.

chapters.n: While Zacharias was serving his turn as priest in the temple…

f.g: Performed his priestly duties.

chapters.n: …he was chosen by lot to burn incense in the Holy Place — an honor that might come only once in a priest’s lifetime.

f.w: his lot was to burn incense
f.g: With thousands of priests, this duty was assigned by casting lots.

chapters.n: Outside, the crowd of worshippers prayed during the incense offering. Rising incense symbolized prayers rising to God.
An angel of the Lord appeared, standing at the right side of the incense altar.

f.g: A small gold altar just before the veil of the Holy of Holies.

chapters.n: Zacharias was startled and overcome with fear.
The angel said: don’t be afraid; your prayer has been heard. Elisabeth will bear you a son, and you will name him John.

f.g: From Hebrew Yohanan, “the Lord is gracious.”

chapters.n: He will bring you joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth.
He will be great before the Lord, will drink no wine or strong drink, and will be filled with the Holy Ghost even before birth.
He will turn many Israelites back to the Lord their God.
He will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, turning hearts of fathers to children and the disobedient to wisdom, to prepare a people ready for the Lord.

f.w: a people prepared for the Lord

chapters.n: Zacharias asked for proof: how can I be sure? I’m old, and so is my wife. His question focused on obstacles rather than God’s promise.
The angel revealed himself: “I am Gabriel, who stands in God’s presence,” sent with good news. Latter-day Saints understand Gabriel to be Noah.

f.g: Hebrew “God is my strength.”
Good news — the same word as “gospel.”

chapters.n: Because he didn’t believe, Zacharias would be unable to speak until the promise came true — a sign and a gentle discipline.

f.g: Unable to speak.

chapters.n: Meanwhile the people outside wondered why he was taking so long in the temple.

f.g: Stayed, delayed.

chapters.n: When he came out, he couldn’t speak or give the usual blessing. He made signs with his hands, and they realized he had seen a vision.

f.g: Made signs, gestured.

chapters.n: When his week of temple service ended, he went home to the hill country.

f.g: Service, period of duty.

chapters.n: Afterward Elisabeth became pregnant and stayed in seclusion for five months.
She praised God: the Lord has looked on me with favor and taken away my public disgrace of childlessness.

f.g: Shame, disgrace.

chapters.n: Six months into Elisabeth’s pregnancy, God sent Gabriel to Nazareth, a small, overlooked village in Galilee.

f.g: A small hill village in lower Galilee.

chapters.n: He came to a virgin named Mary, engaged to Joseph, a descendant of King David.

f.g: Betrothed — a binding engagement, legally like marriage, before the couple lived together.

chapters.n: Gabriel greeted her: “Rejoice, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you.” Mary was chosen by grace.

f.g: A greeting meaning “rejoice” or “greetings.”
Greatly graced by God.

chapters.n: Mary was troubled and thoughtfully wondered what such a greeting could mean. She pondered before reacting.

f.g: Considered, reasoned out.

chapters.n: The angel reassured her: don’t be afraid, Mary; you have found favor with God.
She would conceive and give birth to a son, and name him Jesus.

f.g: Greek form of Hebrew Yeshua (Joshua), “the Lord saves.”

chapters.n: He would be great, called Son of the Most High, and given the throne of his ancestor David — fulfilling God’s covenant with David.

f.w: the throne of his father David

chapters.n: He would reign over Jacob’s house forever; his kingdom would never end.

f.w: of his kingdom there shall be no end

chapters.n: Mary asked how this could happen, since she was a virgin. Unlike Zacharias, she wasn’t asking for proof but for understanding.

f.g: I have not had relations with a man.

chapters.n: The Holy Ghost would come upon her and the power of the Most High would overshadow her, so the holy child would be called the Son of God. Jesus’ divine Father is God himself.
As a sign, Gabriel shared that Mary’s relative Elisabeth, once called barren, was now six months pregnant in her old age.

f.g: Relative, kinswoman — the exact relationship is unknown.

chapters.n: For nothing is impossible with God.

f.w: with God nothing shall be impossible

chapters.n: Mary answered with complete trust: “I am the Lord’s servant. Let it be as you have said.” A model of faithful submission.

f.g: Female servant.

f.w: be it unto me according to thy word

chapters.n: Soon after, Mary hurried to a town in the hill country of Judea.

f.g: Judah, the southern region around Jerusalem.

chapters.n: She entered Zacharias’s home and greeted Elisabeth.

f.g: Greeted.

chapters.n: When Elisabeth heard Mary’s greeting, her unborn baby leaped, and she was filled with the Holy Ghost. Even before birth, John responded to Christ.
She exclaimed loudly: blessed are you among women, and blessed is the child you carry!

f.g: The child she was carrying.

chapters.n: Humbly she asked why she should be honored with a visit from the mother of her Lord. By the Spirit, she already knew who Mary’s child was.
As soon as she heard Mary’s voice, her baby leaped for joy.
Blessed is the woman who believed that the Lord’s promises to her would be fulfilled — a contrast to Zacharias’s doubt.

f.g: Fulfillment.

chapters.n: Mary’s song of praise, the “Magnificat,” begins: my soul magnifies the Lord — declares his greatness. It echoes Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel.

f.g: Make great, glorify. “Magnificat” is the Latin first word of this song.

f.w: My soul doth magnify the Lord

chapters.n: Her spirit rejoices in God her Savior. Even the mother of Jesus needed a Savior.
God noticed the humble status of his servant; from now on every generation will call her blessed.

f.g: Humble condition.

f.w: all generations shall call me blessed

chapters.n: The Mighty One has done great things for her; his name is holy.
God’s mercy extends to every generation of those who reverence him.

f.g: Hold him in reverent awe and respect.

chapters.n: Mary speaks of God’s acts as already done. His powerful arm scatters those who are proud in their thoughts.

f.g: A Hebrew image for God’s power in action.

chapters.n: He brings down rulers from their thrones and lifts up the lowly. God reverses the world’s order.
He fills the hungry with good things and sends the rich away empty.
He has helped his servant Israel, remembering his mercy.

f.g: Helped.

chapters.n: Just as he promised Abraham and his descendants forever. The birth of Jesus fulfills the Abrahamic covenant.

f.w: to Abraham, and to his seed for ever

chapters.n: Mary stayed about three months — likely until John’s birth — then returned home.

f.g: Stayed, remained.

chapters.n: Elisabeth’s time came, and she gave birth to a son.

f.g: Give birth.

chapters.n: Neighbors and relatives heard of the Lord’s great mercy to her and celebrated with her.
On the eighth day they gathered to circumcise the baby and expected to name him Zacharias after his father.

f.g: Circumcision, the sign of the covenant, was performed on the eighth day.

chapters.n: Elisabeth objected: “No, he will be called John.”
They protested that no one in the family had that name. Names usually honored relatives.
They made signs to Zacharias to ask what he wanted — suggesting he may have been deaf as well as mute.
He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” Everyone was amazed. His obedience was now complete.

f.g: A wooden tablet coated with wax for writing.

chapters.n: Immediately he could speak again, and his first words praised God.
Awe fell on the neighbors, and these events became the talk of all the Judean hill country.

f.g: Talked about widely.

chapters.n: Everyone who heard kept wondering, “What will this child become?” The Lord’s hand was clearly with him.

f.w: laid them up in their hearts
f.g: Remembered and pondered them.

chapters.n: Filled with the Holy Ghost, Zacharias prophesied. His song is called the “Benedictus,” from its first Latin word.

f.g: Spoke by inspiration.

chapters.n: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who has come to his people and redeemed them. Zacharias speaks of redemption as already accomplished, so certain is it.

f.g: Came to help — God’s saving presence.
Bought back, freed by paying a price.

chapters.n: God has raised up a mighty Savior from David’s family. The “horn” symbolizes strength, like a powerful animal’s horns.

f.g: A mighty Savior; horns symbolize power.

chapters.n: Just as he promised through his holy prophets from the beginning of the world.
He promised to save us from our enemies and all who hate us.
He has shown the mercy promised to our ancestors and remembered his holy covenant.
The oath he swore to our father Abraham.
That, rescued from our enemies, we could serve him without fear…
…in holiness and righteousness all our lives. The goal of salvation isn’t only rescue but a holy life of service.
Turning to his baby, Zacharias prophesies: you will be called the prophet of the Most High, going before the Lord to prepare his way.
John would teach people how to be saved through the forgiveness of their sins.
All because of God’s tender mercy, by which the sunrise from heaven has come to us — a beautiful name for the Messiah.

f.g: Dawn, sunrise — a title for Christ as the rising light.

chapters.n: He will shine on those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death and guide our feet into the way of peace.
John grew and became strong in spirit and lived in the wilderness until he began his public ministry to Israel. Modern revelation adds that he was ordained by an angel when eight days old.

f.g: Grew, became.

chapters.n: Luke anchors the birth of Jesus in world history. Caesar Augustus, Rome’s first emperor, ordered a registration of everyone in the empire, likely for taxation.

f.g: Octavian, first Roman emperor, ruled 27 BC-AD 14.
Enrolled, registered in a census.

chapters.n: This was the first registration under Quirinius, governor of Syria. The exact dating is debated by historians, but Luke wants readers to know this happened in real history.

f.g: The Greek form of Quirinius, a Roman official over Syria.

chapters.n: Everyone went to their ancestral hometown to register.
Joseph traveled from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem in Judea — David’s hometown — because he was from David’s family line. A Roman decree put Jesus exactly where Micah prophesied he’d be born.

f.g: Hebrew “house of bread,” a village about 6 miles south of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: He went with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was far along in pregnancy. The trip of about 80-90 miles would have been hard for her.

f.g: Heavily pregnant.

chapters.n: While they were in Bethlehem, the time came for her baby to be born.

f.g: Completed, fulfilled.

chapters.n: Mary gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him snugly in strips of cloth, and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no space in the lodging place. The King of kings began life in humble circumstances.

f.g: Strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn.
A feeding trough for animals.
Greek kataluma — a guest room or lodging place, the same word used for the “guestchamber” of the Last Supper.

chapters.n: Nearby, shepherds were living out in the fields, guarding their flocks through the night. Shepherds were humble working men, often looked down on.

f.g: Staying, living.

chapters.n: An angel of the Lord stood before them, and the Lord’s glory blazed around them. They were terrified.

f.g: Very frightened.

chapters.n: The angel said: don’t be afraid — I bring you good news of great joy for all people.
Today in David’s town a Savior has been born for you: he is Christ the Lord. Three titles in one breath: Savior, Messiah, and Lord.

f.w: a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord

chapters.n: The sign: you’ll find a baby wrapped in cloths lying in a feeding trough. A strange sign for a king — and that’s the point.
Suddenly a vast army of heavenly beings joined the angel, praising God.

f.g: The armies of heaven — a great company of angels.

chapters.n: “Glory to God in the highest heaven, and on earth peace and good will toward people.” Christ’s birth brings honor to God and peace to humankind.
When the angels left, the shepherds said: let’s go to Bethlehem and see what the Lord has told us about.
They hurried off and found Mary, Joseph, and the baby lying in the manger, just as promised.
After seeing him, they spread the word about what they had been told about this child. Humble shepherds became the first witnesses of Christ’s birth.
Everyone who heard the shepherds’ story was amazed.
But Mary treasured all these things, quietly turning them over in her heart. Pondering is a pattern for receiving deeper understanding.

f.g: Thought deeply, put things together.

chapters.n: The shepherds went back glorifying and praising God because everything was just as they had been told.
On the eighth day he was circumcised and named Jesus, the name the angel gave before his conception. His parents obeyed both the law and the angel.
After Mary’s forty days of purification under the law, they brought Jesus to the temple in Jerusalem to present him to the Lord.

f.g: A ritual cleansing after childbirth, completed with an offering.

chapters.n: The law said every firstborn son belonged to the Lord, recalling how God spared Israel’s firstborn in Egypt.

f.w: Every male that openeth the womb
f.g: Every firstborn son.

chapters.n: They offered two turtledoves or two young pigeons — the offering allowed for families too poor to afford a lamb. Jesus was born into a family of modest means.

f.w: A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons

chapters.n: In Jerusalem lived Simeon, a righteous, devout man waiting for the comfort God would bring Israel. The Holy Ghost was upon him.

f.g: The comfort and deliverance of Israel through the Messiah.

chapters.n: The Holy Ghost had revealed to him that he would not die before seeing the Lord’s Anointed.

f.g: The Lord’s Messiah, the Anointed One.

chapters.n: Prompted by the Spirit, he came into the temple courts just as Jesus’ parents brought him in to fulfill the law’s requirements. Following a spiritual prompting put him in the right place at the right moment.
Simeon took the baby in his arms and praised God.
His song, called the “Nunc Dimittis,” begins: Lord, now you can let your servant die in peace, as you promised.

f.g: Here, to die — to be released from service.

chapters.n: “My eyes have seen your salvation.” Holding the baby, Simeon held salvation itself.
God prepared this salvation in the sight of all peoples.
Jesus would be a light of revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of Israel — salvation for the whole world, not one nation only.

f.w: A light to lighten the Gentiles

chapters.n: Joseph and Mary marveled at what was said about their son.

f.g: Some ancient manuscripts read “his father and his mother.”

chapters.n: Simeon blessed them and told Mary that the child would cause many in Israel to fall and to rise. He would be a sign that people would oppose. People’s response to Jesus would reveal them.

f.w: the fall and rising again of many

chapters.n: And a sword would pierce Mary’s own soul — a prophecy of her grief at the cross. Through him the hidden thoughts of many would be exposed.

f.w: a sword shall pierce through thy own soul

chapters.n: Anna was also there, a prophetess of the tribe of Asher. She had been married only seven years before her husband died.

f.g: Asher, one of the northern tribes of Israel.

chapters.n: She was a widow of eighty-four (or a widow for eighty-four years) who never left the temple, worshipping night and day with fasting and prayer.

f.g: Eighty-four.

chapters.n: Arriving at that very moment, she thanked God and spoke about the child to everyone waiting for Jerusalem’s redemption. A woman and a man both witness of him, fulfilling the law of witnesses.

f.g: Waited in hope for God to redeem his people.

chapters.n: When they had done everything the law required, they returned home to Nazareth in Galilee. (Matthew adds the visit of the wise men and the flight to Egypt.)
The child grew strong, was filled with wisdom, and God’s grace was on him.

f.g: God’s favor and enabling power.

chapters.n: Every year Jesus’ parents traveled to Jerusalem for Passover — a sign of a faithful family.
When Jesus was twelve, they went up for the feast as usual. A Jewish boy began taking on adult religious duties around this age.
After the festival, as they headed home, Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem without his parents realizing it.

f.g: Stayed behind.

chapters.n: Assuming he was somewhere in the large traveling group, they went a full day’s journey before searching among relatives and friends.

f.g: Caravan, traveling group of families from the same area.

chapters.n: Not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem to look for him.
After three days they found him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers, listening and asking questions. The JST says the teachers were listening to him and asking him questions.

f.g: Teachers of the law, scholars.

f.w: both hearing them, and asking them questions
f.g: JST: “and they were hearing him, and asking him questions.”

chapters.n: Everyone who heard him was astonished at his understanding and his answers.
His parents were shocked. Mary said, “Son, why have you done this to us? Your father and I have been searching for you anxiously.”

f.g: In anguish, distressed.

chapters.n: Jesus’ first recorded words: “Why were you searching? Didn’t you know I must be about my Father’s business?” Gently he pointed to his true Father, God.

f.g: Didn’t you know.
Can also be read “in my Father’s house.”

chapters.n: They didn’t understand what he meant.
He went home to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them. Mary treasured all these things in her heart.

f.g: Obedient to them.

chapters.n: Jesus grew in wisdom (mentally), stature (physically), and favor with God (spiritually) and with people (socially). A balanced pattern for growing up.

Luke dates John’s ministry like a historian, naming the rulers of the time. The fifteenth year of Emperor Tiberius was about AD 28-29. Herod Antipas ruled Galilee, and his brother Philip ruled lands to the northeast.

f.g: Roman emperor AD 14-37, successor of Augustus.
A ruler of part of a kingdom, below the rank of king.

chapters.n: Annas, the former high priest, still held great influence while his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office. Then God’s word came to John in the wilderness — not to the powerful names just listed.

f.g: Annas was deposed by Rome in AD 15 but remained powerful; Caiaphas served about AD 18-36.

f.w: the word of God came unto John

chapters.n: John traveled throughout the Jordan valley, preaching a baptism that showed repentance, for the forgiveness of sins.

f.g: Forgiveness, release from sins.

chapters.n: This fulfilled Isaiah’s words about a voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the Lord’s way. The JST adds a passage here about Christ coming to take away the sins of the world and bring salvation to the Gentiles.

f.w: The voice of one crying in the wilderness

chapters.n: Isaiah pictured road builders preparing a highway for a king: filling valleys, leveling hills, straightening curves. Spiritually, hearts must be made ready for Christ.
Then all humanity will see God’s salvation. Luke, writing for Gentiles, extends the quotation to include this universal promise.

f.g: All people, all humankind.

chapters.n: John spoke bluntly to the crowds: you brood of snakes! Who warned you to run from the coming judgment? He wanted real change, not just a ritual.

f.g: Offspring of poisonous snakes — fleeing a fire, as snakes do from a burning field.

chapters.n: Show by your actions that you’ve truly repented. Don’t rely on being Abraham’s descendants — God could make children of Abraham out of these stones. Lineage alone saves no one.

f.w: We have Abraham to our father

chapters.n: The axe is already at the root. Every tree that doesn’t produce good fruit will be cut down and burned. Judgment is near.

f.w: the axe is laid unto the root

chapters.n: The crowds asked: then what should we do? John’s answers, found only in Luke, are practical.
Share what you have. If you have two shirts, give one to someone who has none; do the same with food. Repentance shows up in generosity.

f.g: Tunics — the basic garment.
Share, give.
Food.

chapters.n: Tax collectors also came to be baptized and asked what they should do.

f.g: Tax collectors, often notorious for overcharging.

chapters.n: Collect no more than you’re required to. Be honest in your work.

f.g: Demand, collect.

chapters.n: Soldiers asked too. John said: don’t extort money by threats or false accusations, and be content with your pay.

f.g: Don’t shake people down for money.

chapters.n: People were filled with expectation, and everyone wondered whether John might be the Messiah.

f.g: Wondered, pondered.

chapters.n: John answered: I baptize with water, but someone far greater is coming — I’m not worthy to untie his sandals. He will baptize with the Holy Ghost and with fire.

f.g: Sandal strap.

f.w: with the Holy Ghost and with fire
f.g: The Spirit purifies like fire.

chapters.n: His winnowing fork is in his hand to clear his threshing floor. He’ll gather the wheat into his barn and burn the chaff — a picture of separating the righteous from the wicked.

f.g: A winnowing fork, used to toss grain so the wind blows away the husks.
Granary, storehouse.
Thoroughly.

chapters.n: With many other appeals, John preached the good news to the people.

f.g: Earnest urging, encouragement.

chapters.n: But Herod Antipas, rebuked by John for marrying his brother’s wife Herodias and for his other evil deeds…

f.g: Rebuked, corrected.

chapters.n: …added this to all his wrongs: he locked John up in prison. Luke tells this before the baptism of Jesus to finish John’s story.
When all the people were being baptized, Jesus was also baptized. While he was praying, heaven opened. Luke often highlights Jesus at prayer.
The Holy Ghost came down on him in bodily form like a dove, and a voice from heaven said, “You are my beloved Son; I am well pleased with you.” Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are all present.

Jesus was about thirty when he began his ministry — the age priests began full service. People assumed he was Joseph’s son; Luke traces the line back through Heli. Many scholars think this genealogy follows Mary’s line or Joseph’s legal line.

f.g: Luke signals that Joseph was not Jesus’ biological father.

chapters.n: Luke’s genealogy runs backward, from Jesus to Adam — unlike Matthew’s, which runs forward from Abraham. These first names are otherwise unknown ancestors from the centuries after the exile.

f.g: One of many little-known names preserved only here.

chapters.n: More unknown ancestors. Their obscurity is part of the message: Jesus came through ordinary families.

f.g: A common Jewish name meaning “gift of the Lord.”

chapters.n: The line continues through ordinary Jews whose names appear nowhere else in scripture.

f.g: Greek form of Shimei.

chapters.n: Zerubbabel and Shealtiel appear — leaders of the Jews who returned from Babylon and rebuilt the temple. They are also in Matthew’s list.

f.g: Zerubbabel, governor who led the rebuilding of the temple after the exile.
Shealtiel.

chapters.n: These names reach back into the period of the kings of Judah and the exile, though not through the royal line.

f.g: Not the same as Judah’s son Er in Genesis.

chapters.n: Another run of names, including Joshua (Jose) and another Levi, otherwise unrecorded.

f.g: A form of Joshua/Jesus.

chapters.n: Names here echo the tribal patriarchs — Simeon, Judah, Joseph — common names among faithful Israelite families.
Luke traces Jesus through Nathan, a son of David, rather than through Solomon and the kings as Matthew does. Either way, Jesus is a true son of David.

f.g: A son of David and Bathsheba, brother of Solomon.

chapters.n: From David back through Jesse, Obed, and Boaz (husband of Ruth), to Salmon and Nahshon, a leader of Judah in Moses’ day.

f.g: Boaz, who married Ruth the Moabite.
Nahshon, chief of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness.

chapters.n: Back through the tribe of Judah: Amminadab, Ram, Hezron, Perez, and Judah himself, son of Jacob.

f.g: Perez, son of Judah and Tamar.

chapters.n: The covenant patriarchs: Jacob, Isaac, Abraham, then Terah and Nahor. Jesus is the promised seed of Abraham.

f.g: Terah, Abraham’s father.

chapters.n: Before Abraham, the line runs through the descendants of Shem listed in Genesis: Serug, Reu, Peleg, Eber (ancestor of the Hebrews), and Shelah.

f.g: Eber, possibly the source of the name “Hebrew.”

chapters.n: Here Luke includes a second Cainan between Arphaxad and Shelah, following the Greek Old Testament. Then Shem, Noah, and Lamech.

f.g: This Cainan appears in the Greek Septuagint version of Genesis 11 but not the Hebrew text.
Noah.

chapters.n: The antediluvian (pre-flood) patriarchs: Methuselah, Enoch, Jared, Mahalaleel, and Cainan (Kenan). Latter-day Saint scripture tells much more about Enoch and his city of Zion.

f.g: Methuselah.

chapters.n: Finally Enos, Seth, Adam — and God. By tracing Jesus to Adam, “the son of God,” Luke shows that Jesus came for all of humanity, not just Israel.

f.w: Adam, which was the son of God

chapters.n: Full of the Holy Ghost after his baptism, Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness. Being filled with the Spirit doesn’t exempt anyone from trials — it prepares us for them.

f.w: led by the Spirit into the wilderness

chapters.n: For forty days he ate nothing, and at the end he was hungry. The JST clarifies that the devil came to tempt him after the forty days, which Jesus had spent communing with God.
The devil’s first temptation targeted physical hunger and questioned his identity: “If you are the Son of God,” turn this stone into bread. Satan often attacks who we are.

f.w: If thou be the Son of God
f.g: The Greek implies “since you are” — tempting him to use his power selfishly.

chapters.n: Jesus answered with scripture: people don’t live by bread alone. Spiritual nourishment from God matters more than physical comfort.

f.w: man shall not live by bread alone

chapters.n: The devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world in an instant. The JST says it was the Spirit, not the devil, who took Jesus up the mountain.

f.g: In an instant — a visionary view.

chapters.n: Satan offered all their power and glory, claiming it had been given to him to hand out. He is a liar; his “gifts” always cost the soul.
The price: worship me, and it will all be yours. A shortcut to a crown that bypassed the cross.
Jesus refused: “Get behind me, Satan.” Scripture says to worship and serve only the Lord God.

f.w: Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God

chapters.n: The setting moved to the highest corner of the temple in Jerusalem. If you’re the Son of God, jump. (The JST again has the Spirit bringing Jesus there.)

f.g: A high point of the temple complex, perhaps overlooking the Kidron Valley.

chapters.n: This time Satan quoted scripture himself: God will command his angels to protect you. Scripture can be twisted to serve wrong purposes.

f.w: He shall give his angels charge over thee

chapters.n: The quote continues: they will carry you so you won’t even hurt your foot on a stone.
Jesus answered with scripture in context: don’t put the Lord your God to the test. Forcing God to prove himself isn’t faith.

f.w: Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God

chapters.n: When the devil finished every temptation, he left — but only until another opportunity. Temptation returns; resistance must continue.

f.g: Until an opportune time.

chapters.n: Jesus returned to Galilee in the Spirit’s power, and news about him spread throughout the region.

f.g: Report, news.

chapters.n: He taught in their synagogues, and everyone praised him — at first.
He came to Nazareth, his hometown, and on the sabbath went to the synagogue, as was his habit, and stood up to read. Jesus made regular worship a custom.
He was handed the scroll of Isaiah, unrolled it, and found the passage he wanted.

f.g: A scroll, unrolled to the right place.
Isaiah.

chapters.n: He read Isaiah 61: the Lord’s Spirit is upon me; he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor, heal broken hearts, free captives, give sight to the blind, and liberate the oppressed. This was his mission statement.

f.w: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me

f.g: The root of “Messiah” and “Christ” — the Anointed One.

chapters.n: And to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor — the jubilee, when debts were forgiven and slaves freed.

f.g: A year of God’s favor, echoing the jubilee year of release.

chapters.n: He rolled up the scroll, handed it to the attendant, and sat down — the posture of a teacher. Everyone stared at him.

f.g: The synagogue attendant who cared for the scrolls.
Fixed intently.

chapters.n: Then he said: today this scripture is fulfilled as you listen. He was claiming to be the Anointed One Isaiah described.

f.w: This day is this scripture fulfilled

chapters.n: At first everyone spoke well of him and marveled at his gracious words, but they asked, “Isn’t this Joseph’s son?” Familiarity began turning to doubt.

f.g: Words full of grace and charm.

chapters.n: Jesus knew their thoughts: they would quote the proverb, “Doctor, heal yourself” — prove it by doing the miracles here that you did in Capernaum.

f.g: A proverb challenging him to prove himself at home.

chapters.n: He told them plainly that no prophet is accepted in his own hometown.

f.w: No prophet is accepted in his own country

chapters.n: He reminded them that in Elijah’s day, during a famine of three and a half years, there were many widows in Israel…

f.g: Elijah.

chapters.n: …but Elijah was sent to none of them — only to a Gentile widow in Zarephath, near Sidon.

f.g: Zarephath, a Phoenician town.

chapters.n: And in Elisha’s day there were many lepers in Israel, but only Naaman the Syrian — a foreign army commander — was healed. God’s blessings come to those with faith, whatever their nation.

f.g: Elisha.

chapters.n: Hearing that God had blessed Gentiles over Israelites, everyone in the synagogue was furious.

f.g: Rage.

chapters.n: They drove him out of town to the edge of the hill Nazareth was built on, intending to throw him off the cliff. The adoring audience became a lynch mob.

f.g: The edge of a cliff.

chapters.n: But he walked right through the crowd and went on his way. His time to die had not yet come.

f.w: passing through the midst of them

chapters.n: He went down to Capernaum, a town in Galilee, and taught there on the sabbath.

f.g: A lakeside town lower in elevation than hilly Nazareth — hence “came down.”

chapters.n: People were amazed at his teaching, because his message carried authority and power.
In the synagogue, a man possessed by an evil spirit screamed out loudly.

f.g: An evil, impure spirit.

chapters.n: “Leave us alone! What do you want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are — the Holy One of God.” The demon knew exactly who Jesus was.
Jesus rebuked it: “Be quiet and come out!” The demon threw the man down in front of everyone and left without hurting him.

f.g: Be silent.

chapters.n: Everyone was amazed: what kind of word is this? With authority and power he commands evil spirits, and they leave!
News about him spread throughout the surrounding area.
Leaving the synagogue, he went to Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law had a high fever, and they asked him to help her. Luke, a physician, notes the fever was “great.”

f.g: A medical term for a severe fever — fitting for Luke, “the beloved physician.”

chapters.n: He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left. She got up at once and served them.

f.g: Served them, perhaps preparing a meal.

chapters.n: At sunset, when the sabbath ended, people brought all their sick to him. He laid his hands on each one individually and healed them. He ministered one by one.

f.w: laid his hands on every one of them

f.g: Various.

chapters.n: Demons came out of many, shouting, “You are the Christ, the Son of God!” He rebuked them and wouldn’t let them speak, because they knew he was the Messiah.

f.g: Did not allow them.

chapters.n: At daybreak he went to a solitary place. The crowds searched for him and tried to keep him from leaving.

f.g: Tried to hold him back.

chapters.n: He explained: I must proclaim the good news of God’s kingdom to other towns too — that’s why I was sent.
And he kept preaching in the synagogues of Galilee (some manuscripts read Judea, meaning the Jewish homeland in general).
Crowds pressed in to hear God’s word as Jesus stood beside the Lake of Gennesaret — Luke’s name for the Sea of Galilee.

f.g: The Sea of Galilee, named for the fertile plain on its northwest shore.

chapters.n: He noticed two boats pulled up on shore. The fishermen had stepped out and were cleaning their nets after a fruitless night.
Jesus got into Simon’s boat and asked him to push out a little from shore. Sitting down, he taught the crowd from the boat — the water carried his voice.

f.g: Asked him.

chapters.n: When he finished, he told Simon to head out into deep water and lower the nets for a catch.

f.g: A haul or catch of fish.

chapters.n: Simon, the expert fisherman, explained they had worked hard all night and caught nothing. Still, because Jesus said so, he would do it. Obedience before understanding.
They caught such an enormous number of fish that their nets began to tear.

f.g: Enclosed, caught.

chapters.n: They signaled their partners in the other boat to come help. Both boats were filled so full they started to sink.
Simon Peter fell at Jesus’ knees: “Go away from me, Lord — I am a sinful man.” In the presence of divine power, Peter suddenly saw his own unworthiness.
He and everyone with him were stunned by the catch.
So were James and John, Zebedee’s sons, Simon’s business partners. Jesus told Simon: don’t be afraid; from now on you will catch people.

f.g: Greek: “catch alive” — rescue people, not trap them.

chapters.n: They brought the boats ashore, left everything — even the greatest catch of their lives — and followed him.
In one of the towns, a man covered with leprosy saw Jesus, fell face down, and pleaded: Lord, if you’re willing, you can make me clean. Luke the physician notes the disease was advanced.

f.g: Covered with the disease — an advanced case.

chapters.n: Jesus reached out and touched him: “I am willing. Be clean.” Instantly the leprosy was gone. He touched the untouchable.
He told him not to tell anyone, but to show himself to the priest and offer what Moses required for cleansing, as evidence to them.
Still, news about him spread even more, and huge crowds gathered to hear him and be healed.

f.g: Weaknesses, illnesses.

chapters.n: But he would often slip away to lonely places to pray. Luke shows that busy ministry and private prayer went together for Jesus.

f.w: withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed

chapters.n: One day while he taught, Pharisees and teachers of the law from all over Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem were sitting there, and the Lord’s power to heal was with him.

f.g: Teachers and experts in the law of Moses.

chapters.n: Some men carried a paralyzed man on a mat and tried to bring him in and lay him before Jesus.

f.g: Paralysis.

chapters.n: Unable to get through the crowd, they climbed onto the roof and lowered him on his mat through the tiles right in front of Jesus. Luke, writing for Greek readers, describes a tiled roof.

f.g: Roof tiles.

chapters.n: Seeing their faith, Jesus said, “Friend, your sins are forgiven.” He healed the soul first.
The scribes and Pharisees began to object inwardly: who is this who speaks blasphemy? Only God can forgive sins.

f.g: Words that dishonor God or claim his prerogatives.

chapters.n: Jesus knew what they were thinking and asked why they reasoned that way in their hearts.
Which is easier to say: “Your sins are forgiven” or “Get up and walk”? One can be checked; the other can’t.
To prove the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he told the paralyzed man: get up, take your mat, and go home.
At once the man stood up in front of them, picked up his mat, and went home praising God. The healing confirmed the forgiveness.
Everyone was amazed, praised God, and was filled with awe: we’ve seen remarkable things today.

f.g: Extraordinary, unexpected things — Greek paradoxa.

chapters.n: Afterward Jesus saw a tax collector named Levi at his tax booth and said, “Follow me.”

f.g: Tax booth.
Also called Matthew.

chapters.n: Levi left everything, got up, and followed him. For a tax collector, leaving his post meant there was likely no going back.
Levi threw a big banquet for Jesus at his home, and many tax collectors and others ate with them. His first act as a disciple was to introduce his friends to Jesus.
The Pharisees and their scribes complained to his disciples: why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?

f.g: Grumbled.

chapters.n: Jesus answered: healthy people don’t need a doctor; sick people do.

f.g: Healthy, well.

chapters.n: He came to call sinners to repentance, not those who think they are righteous. Only Luke adds “to repentance” — he calls people to change, not just to company.
They then asked why John’s disciples and the Pharisees’ followers often fast and pray, but his disciples eat and drink.

f.g: Offer formal, set prayers.

chapters.n: Jesus asked: can you make wedding guests fast while the groom is still with them?

f.g: Wedding guests, the groom’s attendants.

chapters.n: But the time will come when the groom is taken away, and then they will fast. An early hint of his death.
He gave a comparison: no one tears a patch from a new garment to fix an old one. That ruins the new one, and the patch won’t match the old.

f.g: Tear.

chapters.n: No one pours new wine into old wineskins; the fermenting wine would burst them, and both wine and skins would be lost.

f.g: Wineskins made of animal hide.

chapters.n: New wine needs fresh skins, so both are preserved. The new covenant needs hearts willing to be made new.
Only Luke adds this: people who have drunk old wine don’t want new; they say the old is better. A gentle explanation of why many resisted Jesus’ new teaching.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “the old is good” — content with what they already have.

chapters.n: On a sabbath, Jesus walked through grain fields, and his disciples picked heads of grain, rubbed off the husks in their hands, and ate. Luke’s detail shows exactly what the Pharisees called “work.”

f.g: An unclear phrase in the Greek; many manuscripts simply say “a sabbath.”
Grain (wheat or barley).

chapters.n: Some Pharisees challenged them: why are you doing what is forbidden on the sabbath? To them, plucking was reaping and rubbing was threshing.
Jesus answered: haven’t you read what David did when he and his men were hungry?

f.g: Hungry.

chapters.n: David entered God’s house and ate the consecrated bread meant only for priests, and shared it with his men. Mercy and need can outweigh ritual rules.

f.g: The “bread of the Presence,” twelve loaves placed before the Lord.

chapters.n: And he declared that the Son of Man is Lord of the sabbath — he has authority over the day he himself established.
On another sabbath he taught in a synagogue where there was a man whose right hand was withered. Luke the physician notes which hand — the one needed for work.

f.g: Shriveled, paralyzed.

chapters.n: The scribes and Pharisees watched closely to see if he would heal on the sabbath, looking for grounds to accuse him.
Jesus knew their thoughts and told the man to get up and stand in front of everyone. He did.
Jesus asked them: is it lawful on the sabbath to do good or harm, to save a life or destroy it? Their plotting that very day was itself the real sabbath-breaking.
Looking around at them all, he told the man to stretch out his hand. He did, and it was completely restored.
They were filled with fury and discussed what they could do to Jesus.

f.g: Senseless rage.
Talked, conferred.

chapters.n: Jesus went up into the hills and spent the entire night praying to God. He prepared for an important decision through long prayer.
At daybreak he called his disciples and chose twelve of them, naming them apostles — “ones sent forth.”

f.g: Greek apostolos, a messenger sent with authority.

chapters.n: The list: Simon, whom he named Peter, and his brother Andrew; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew.

f.g: Often thought to be Nathanael.

chapters.n: Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, and Simon the Zealot — possibly once part of a movement opposed to Rome. A former tax collector and a zealot served side by side.

f.g: “The Zealot” — someone zealous for the law, perhaps tied to anti-Roman nationalists.

chapters.n: Judas son (or brother) of James, also called Thaddaeus, and Judas Iscariot, who became the traitor.

f.g: The Greek says only “Judas of James,” usually meaning son of James.

chapters.n: Coming down, he stood on a level place with many disciples and a huge crowd from Judea, Jerusalem, and the coast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and be healed. Luke’s version of Jesus’ great sermon is called the “Sermon on the Plain.”

f.g: A level place, perhaps a plateau on the mountainside.

chapters.n: Those troubled by evil spirits were also healed.

f.g: Tormented, harassed.

chapters.n: The whole crowd tried to touch him, because power was going out from him and healing them all.

f.g: Power.

chapters.n: Looking at his disciples, he said: blessed are you who are poor, for God’s kingdom is yours. Luke’s beatitudes speak directly (“you”) and include real poverty. Matthew adds “in spirit.”
Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh. God will reverse present sorrows.
Blessed are you when people hate you, exclude you, insult you, and reject your name as evil because of the Son of Man.

f.w: cast out your name as evil
f.g: Slander your reputation, perhaps expel you from the synagogue.

chapters.n: Rejoice and jump for joy then, because your reward in heaven is great — their ancestors treated the prophets the same way.
Luke adds four “woes” that mirror the blessings. Woe to you who are rich — you have already received your comfort.

f.g: An expression of grief and warning — “how sad for you.”
Comfort — they’ve had their reward already.

chapters.n: Woe to you who are full now — you will be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now — you will mourn and weep.
Woe to you when everyone praises you — that’s how their ancestors treated false prophets. Popularity is not a sign of truth.

f.w: when all men shall speak well of you

chapters.n: To those willing to listen: love your enemies and do good to those who hate you. This is the heart of Christian discipleship.
Bless those who curse you and pray for those who mistreat you.

f.g: Mistreat, abuse, insult you.

chapters.n: If someone strikes your cheek, offer the other. If someone takes your outer cloak, don’t withhold your tunic. Refuse to retaliate.

f.g: Outer robe.
Inner tunic.

chapters.n: Give to everyone who asks, and don’t demand back what someone takes. Generosity over grasping.

f.w: Give to every man that asketh of thee

chapters.n: Treat others the way you want them to treat you — the “Golden Rule.”

f.w: as ye would that men should do to you

chapters.n: If you only love those who love you, what credit is that? Even sinners do that.

f.g: What credit or favor is that to you?

chapters.n: If you only do good to people who do good to you, what credit is that? Sinners do the same.
If you lend only when you expect repayment, what credit is that? Even sinners lend to sinners expecting full repayment.

Love your enemies, do good, and lend without expecting anything back. Your reward will be great, and you’ll be children of the Most High, who is kind even to the ungrateful and wicked. We become like God by loving as he loves.
Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful. Luke’s version of Matthew’s “be perfect” centers on mercy.
Don’t judge, and you won’t be judged. Don’t condemn, and you won’t be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven.

f.g: The JST of the parallel adds: judge not unrighteously.

f.w: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven

chapters.n: Give, and you will receive — a full measure, pressed down, shaken to settle, and overflowing into your lap. The measure you use will be used for you.

f.g: The fold of a robe above the belt, used like a pocket to carry grain.
Measure out with.

chapters.n: He gave a comparison: can a blind person guide a blind person? Won’t they both fall into a pit? Choose guides who can truly see.

f.w: Can the blind lead the blind?

chapters.n: A student isn’t above the teacher, but a fully trained student will become like the teacher. Disciples become like whom they follow.

f.g: Fully trained, complete.

chapters.n: Why notice the speck of sawdust in someone else’s eye but ignore the plank in your own? A humorous picture of hypocrisy.

f.g: A speck, a tiny splinter.
A large wooden beam or plank.

chapters.n: How can you offer to remove your brother’s speck while ignoring your own plank? Hypocrite — first remove your own; then you’ll see clearly to help him. Self-correction comes before correcting others.

f.w: cast out first the beam out of thine own eye

chapters.n: A good tree doesn’t produce rotten fruit, and a rotten tree doesn’t produce good fruit.

f.g: Rotten, worthless.

chapters.n: Each tree is recognized by its fruit. You don’t pick figs from thorns or grapes from brambles. Character shows in actions.

f.w: every tree is known by his own fruit

chapters.n: Good people bring good things out of the good stored in their hearts; evil people bring out evil. What fills the heart comes out of the mouth.

f.w: of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh

chapters.n: Why call me “Lord, Lord” and not do what I say? Words without obedience are empty.
Jesus describes someone who comes to him, hears his words, and acts on them.
That person is like a builder who dug deep and laid the foundation on rock. When the flood came and the torrent crashed against the house, it couldn’t shake it.

f.w: laid the foundation on a rock

f.g: With great force.

chapters.n: But the one who hears and doesn’t act is like someone who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the torrent hit, it collapsed at once, and its ruin was complete.
After finishing his sermon to the people, Jesus went back to Capernaum, his home base.

f.w: in the audience of the people
f.g: In the hearing of the people.

chapters.n: A Roman centurion there had a servant he valued highly, who was sick and about to die. This officer cared deeply about someone society considered property.

f.g: A Roman army officer over about 100 soldiers — here likely serving Herod Antipas.
Highly valued, precious to him.

chapters.n: Hearing about Jesus, he sent some Jewish elders to ask Jesus to come heal his servant. As a Gentile, he approached respectfully through local leaders.

f.g: Respected leaders of the local Jewish community.

chapters.n: The elders pleaded earnestly with Jesus, saying this man deserved his help.

f.g: Earnestly, urgently.

chapters.n: He loves our nation and even built our synagogue for us. Here was a Gentile who had blessed God’s people.

f.w: he hath built us a synagogue
f.g: Remains of a later synagogue in Capernaum stand on what may be the foundation of an earlier one.

chapters.n: Jesus went with them. Near the house, the centurion sent friends with a message: Lord, don’t trouble yourself — I’m not worthy to have you under my roof. He knew a Jew might become ritually unclean entering a Gentile home.
That’s why I didn’t come to you myself. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed. He believed Jesus’ word alone had power, even at a distance.

f.g: Simply speak the command.

chapters.n: He explained: I understand authority. I’m under orders myself, and I have soldiers under me who go and come when I command. He recognized that Jesus held authority over sickness.
Jesus was amazed. He turned to the crowd and said he hadn’t found such great faith even in Israel. Faith can be found in unexpected places.

f.g: Was astonished.

chapters.n: When the messengers returned to the house, they found the servant completely healthy.

f.g: Healthy, fully recovered.

chapters.n: The next day Jesus went to Nain, a village southwest of the Sea of Galilee, followed by his disciples and a large crowd.

f.g: A village near Mount Tabor, about 6 miles southeast of Nazareth.

chapters.n: At the town gate they met a funeral procession. The dead man was his mother’s only son, and she was a widow. Without husband or son, she faced grief and likely poverty. Many townspeople were with her.

f.w: the only son of his mother

chapters.n: When the Lord saw her, his heart went out to her, and he said, “Don’t cry.” No one asked him to help; his compassion moved him first.
He stepped forward and touched the open coffin, and the bearers stood still. He said, “Young man, I tell you, get up!”

f.g: An open stretcher or frame used to carry the dead to burial.

chapters.n: The dead man sat up and began to talk, and Jesus gave him back to his mother — words echoing Elijah’s miracle for another widow.

f.w: he delivered him to his mother

chapters.n: Awe swept over everyone. They praised God, saying a great prophet had appeared among them and God had come to help his people.
The news about him spread throughout Judea and all the surrounding region.

f.g: Report, news (not necessarily untrue).

chapters.n: John’s disciples reported all these things to John, who was in prison.

f.g: Told, reported.

chapters.n: John sent two of his disciples to ask Jesus: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for someone else?” Many think John sent them so his followers could see for themselves.

f.g: A title for the expected Messiah.

chapters.n: The two delivered John’s question word for word.
Right then Jesus healed many of illnesses, afflictions, and evil spirits, and gave sight to many blind people.

f.g: Painful afflictions.

chapters.n: His answer was to point to the evidence: go tell John what you’ve seen and heard — the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor hear good news. These were Isaiah’s signs of the Messiah.
And blessed is anyone who doesn’t stumble over me — who isn’t put off because I don’t fit their expectations.

f.g: Caused to stumble, to fall away.

chapters.n: After the messengers left, Jesus spoke about John: what did you go out to the desert to see? A reed blowing in the wind? John was no flimsy, wavering man.

f.w: A reed shaken with the wind
f.g: Reeds grew along the Jordan; the image suggests someone easily swayed.

chapters.n: A man in fancy clothes? People who dress in luxury live in palaces — where John was now a prisoner, not a courtier.

f.g: Live in luxury.

chapters.n: A prophet? Yes — and much more than a prophet.
He is the one Malachi wrote about: the messenger sent ahead to prepare the way.

f.w: I send my messenger before thy face

chapters.n: No one born of a woman is greater than John. Yet the least in God’s kingdom is greater than he. Joseph Smith taught that the one “least” in the kingdom referred to Jesus himself.

f.w: there is not a greater prophet than John the Baptist

chapters.n: The ordinary people and even tax collectors who heard this acknowledged that God’s way was right, since they had been baptized by John.

f.g: Declared God to be right, accepted his plan.

chapters.n: But the Pharisees and experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for them by refusing John’s baptism. Rejecting God’s servants means rejecting God’s plan for ourselves.

f.w: rejected the counsel of God against themselves

f.g: Experts in the law of Moses, not courtroom attorneys.

chapters.n: Jesus asked: how can I describe the people of this generation? What are they like?

f.g: To what.

chapters.n: They’re like children in the marketplace complaining to each other: we played the flute and you wouldn’t dance; we sang a funeral song and you wouldn’t cry. Nothing pleases them.

f.g: Played the flute — as at a wedding.

chapters.n: John came fasting and abstaining from wine, and you said he had a demon.

f.w: neither eating bread nor drinking wine

chapters.n: The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you call him a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners. Critics will find fault no matter what.

f.g: Heavy drinker.

f.w: a friend of publicans and sinners
f.g: Meant as an insult, but a beautiful truth about Jesus.

chapters.n: But God’s wisdom is proven right by all who follow it. The results in people’s lives show who was wise.

f.w: wisdom is justified of all her children

chapters.n: A Pharisee named Simon invited Jesus to dinner. Jesus accepted and reclined at the table. Jesus ate with Pharisees as well as sinners.

f.g: Reclined at the meal, lying on a couch with feet stretched away from the table.

chapters.n: A woman in that town known as a sinner learned Jesus was eating there and came with an alabaster jar of perfume. Banquets were semi-public, so onlookers could enter.

f.g: A flask of perfumed oil carved from soft stone.
Probably someone with a publicly known immoral past; Luke doesn’t name her.

chapters.n: She stood behind him at his feet, weeping. Her tears fell on his feet; she wiped them with her hair, kissed his feet, and anointed them with the perfume. Her actions poured out repentance and gratitude.

f.w: wipe them with the hairs of her head
f.g: Letting down her hair in public was considered shocking — she cared more about honoring him than her reputation.

chapters.n: The host thought to himself: if this man were a prophet, he’d know what kind of woman is touching him — a sinner. He assumed a holy man would avoid her.

f.g: Had invited him.

chapters.n: Jesus, reading his thoughts, said, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” “Go ahead, Teacher.” Jesus proved he was a prophet by knowing Simon’s mind.

f.g: Something.

chapters.n: A moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii (about a year and a half of wages); the other owed fifty.

f.g: Denarii; one was about a day’s wage.

chapters.n: Neither could repay, so he generously canceled both debts. Which one will love him more?

f.g: Freely, graciously.

chapters.n: Simon answered, “I suppose the one who was forgiven more.” Jesus said, “You have judged correctly.”
Turning to the woman, Jesus said: Simon, do you see this woman? You didn’t give me water to wash my feet — a basic courtesy — but she washed them with her tears and dried them with her hair.

f.w: thou gavest me no water for my feet
f.g: Hosts normally offered water to wash dusty feet.

chapters.n: You didn’t greet me with a kiss, but she hasn’t stopped kissing my feet since I came in.

f.g: A kiss on the cheek was the customary greeting for a guest.

chapters.n: You didn’t anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with perfume.

f.w: My head with oil thou didst not anoint

chapters.n: So her many sins have been forgiven — her great love shows it. But whoever is forgiven little loves little. Recognizing our need for forgiveness deepens our love for the Savior.

f.g: Her love is the evidence of forgiveness, not the payment for it, as the parable shows.

f.w: Her sins, which are many, are forgiven

chapters.n: Then Jesus said to her directly, “Your sins are forgiven.” He spoke the words she most needed to hear.
The other guests began asking among themselves: who is this who even forgives sins?
Jesus told the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” She left with a new life. Faith in Christ brings forgiveness and peace.
Jesus keeps moving from town to town with a traveling missionary company. The good news (“glad tidings”) is that God’s kingdom has drawn near in Him, and the Twelve are learning by being at His side.

f.g: The Greek word behind this is the root of “evangel” or “gospel” — good news.

chapters.n: Luke alone names the women who traveled with Jesus. Many had been healed by Him, and their gratitude turned into discipleship. Mary Magdalene, freed from seven devils, later becomes the first witness of the risen Lord.

f.g: From Magdala, a fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.

chapters.n: These women used their own money and goods to support Jesus and the Twelve. Joanna came from Herod Antipas’s own household, showing the gospel reaching even into the palace of the ruler of Galilee.

f.g: A manager of a household or estate — Chuza ran Herod’s affairs.
Out of their own possessions and means.

chapters.n: A huge crowd gathers from many towns, and Jesus teaches them with a parable — a short story from everyday life that carries a deeper spiritual lesson for those willing to seek it.

f.g: Greek parabolē, “a placing side by side” — a comparison that teaches by likeness.

chapters.n: Farmers in Galilee scattered seed by hand, so some landed on the hard footpaths between fields. Trampled by travelers and eaten by birds, it never had a chance to grow.

f.w: A sower went out to sow his seed

f.g: Birds.

chapters.n: Some seed fell where a thin layer of soil covered rock. It sprouted quickly, but with no depth to hold water its roots dried up and the plant died.

f.g: Matthew and Mark say it “had no root” and “no deepness of earth.”

chapters.n: Other seed landed in ground already full of thorn roots. Both grew together, but the thorns crowded out the grain and smothered it.

f.g: Strangled — deprived of light and space to grow.

chapters.n: Good soil produced a bumper harvest, a hundred times what was planted. Jesus then calls out a challenge: truly listen, and let the message sink in.

f.w: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear

f.g: A hundred times as much — an extraordinary, almost miraculous yield.

chapters.n: The disciples don’t pretend to understand. They ask. Their humble question opens the way for Jesus to explain, a pattern for anyone who studies the scriptures.
Parables both reveal and conceal. Those who seek receive the deeper meaning; those who don’t care hear only a story. God gives light as people are ready to receive it.

f.g: In the New Testament, truths that can only be known by revelation, not secrets kept from the faithful.

chapters.n: Jesus gives the key to the parable: the seed is God’s word. The story is really about different kinds of hearts and how they receive that word.

f.w: The seed is the word of God

chapters.n: The hard pathway is a heart that hears but never lets the word in. Before it can take root, the devil snatches it away so that it never leads to faith.

f.g: Greek diabolos, “accuser” or “slanderer.”

chapters.n: Rocky ground describes people who receive the gospel with excitement but never put down roots. When trials come, their shallow faith withers.

f.g: Here mainly testing or trial — pressures that reveal what a person’s faith is made of.

chapters.n: The thorny ground is a crowded life. Worries, wealth, and pleasures aren’t always evil in themselves, but they can slowly squeeze out spiritual growth until nothing ripens.

f.g: Their fruit never fully ripens — growth starts but never matures.

chapters.n: Good soil is an honest heart that hears, holds on, and keeps going. The fruit comes with patience — steady endurance over time, not instant results.

f.g: Greek kalos and agathos — noble and good; a sincere, well-prepared heart.

chapters.n: A lamp is meant to be seen. The light Jesus gives His disciples isn’t meant to be hidden but shared, so that others coming in can see too.

f.g: Really a small clay oil lamp, the common light source of the time.
A lampstand that held the lamp up so it lit the whole room.

chapters.n: Truth will not stay hidden forever. What God is teaching quietly now will one day be openly known, and every hidden thing will finally come to light.
How we listen matters. Those who use the light they receive are given more; those who neglect it lose even what they thought they had.

f.w: whosoever hath, to him shall be given

chapters.n: Mary and Jesus’ brothers come to see Him, but the crowd is so thick they cannot reach Him.

f.g: The crowd pressing in on every side.

chapters.n: Someone passes word through the crowd that His family is waiting outside.

f.g: Outside.

chapters.n: Jesus does not reject His family; He widens it. Everyone who hears God’s word and lives it becomes part of His true family.

f.w: hear the word of God, and do it

chapters.n: Jesus and His disciples set out by boat to cross the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake about 13 miles long.

f.g: Luke, who wrote for a Greek audience, calls it a lake rather than a sea — the Sea of Galilee.

chapters.n: Worn out, Jesus falls asleep. The lake sits low among hills, and sudden violent winds can sweep down onto it. Waves fill the boat and the crew is in real danger.

f.g: Danger.

chapters.n: The terrified disciples wake Him. With a word He rebukes the wind and waves, and the storm stops at once — a calm as sudden as the storm itself.
Jesus gently asks where their faith went. Their fear shifts from the storm to awe at Him: who can command nature itself? The answer is that the Creator is in the boat.

f.w: What manner of man is this!

chapters.n: They land on the eastern shore, opposite Galilee, in largely Gentile territory known as the Decapolis.

f.g: Ancient manuscripts vary (Gadarenes, Gerasenes, Gergesenes); all refer to the region southeast of the lake.

chapters.n: A man possessed for a long time meets them. He lives naked among the tombs, cut off from home and society — a picture of how completely evil can isolate and degrade a person.

f.g: Burial caves in hillsides; places Jews considered ritually unclean.

chapters.n: The evil spirits recognize Jesus immediately and name Him as the Son of the Most High God. They know who He is, and they fear His power.

f.w: What have I to do with thee
f.g: An idiom meaning “What do we have in common?” or “Leave me alone.”

chapters.n: Luke explains the backstory: Jesus had already ordered the spirit out. The man had been chained repeatedly, but he broke every restraint and was driven into the wilderness.

f.g: Shackles for the feet.

chapters.n: When Jesus asks his name, the answer is “Legion,” because so many devils had entered him.

f.g: A Roman army unit of several thousand soldiers — here meaning a vast number.

chapters.n: The spirits beg not to be sent into “the deep,” showing that even devils must submit to Christ’s authority.

f.g: Greek abyssos, the abyss — a place of confinement for evil spirits.

chapters.n: A large herd of pigs is grazing nearby — likely owned by Gentiles, since Jews considered swine unclean. The devils ask to enter them, and Jesus allows it.

f.g: Allowed.

chapters.n: The devils leave the man and enter the herd, which rushes down a steep slope into the lake and drowns. Their destructive nature is laid bare.

f.g: Drowned.

chapters.n: The herdsmen flee and spread the news through the town and countryside.

f.g: The herdsmen who tended the pigs.

chapters.n: People come and find the once-wild man sitting calmly at Jesus’ feet, dressed and sane. Yet instead of rejoicing, they are afraid.

f.w: sitting at the feet of Jesus
f.g: The posture of a disciple learning from a teacher.

chapters.n: Eyewitnesses explain how the possessed man was healed.

f.g: Controlled by evil spirits.

chapters.n: Overwhelmed with fear — and perhaps worried about their loss of property — the people ask Jesus to leave. He respects their choice and goes.

f.g: Begged Him to leave.

chapters.n: The healed man wants to stay with Jesus, but Jesus has a different mission for him.

f.g: Begged Him.

chapters.n: Jesus sends him home as a witness to his own people. Notice: Jesus says “God” did this, and the man tells what “Jesus” did — the two are united in the work.

f.g: Proclaimed openly.

chapters.n: Back on the Galilean side, a crowd is eagerly waiting for Jesus — a sharp contrast to the people who asked Him to leave.

f.g: Welcomed Him.

chapters.n: Jairus, a respected synagogue leader, sets aside his status and falls at Jesus’ feet, pleading for Him to come to his home.

f.g: A lay leader who arranged worship services in the local synagogue.

chapters.n: His only daughter, about twelve, is dying. As Jesus goes with him, the crowd presses in so closely He can barely move.

f.g: Was dying.
Crowded around and pressed against.

chapters.n: A woman has suffered bleeding for twelve years — as long as Jairus’s daughter has been alive. She has spent everything on doctors with no cure.

f.g: A chronic hemorrhage; under the law of Moses it also made her ritually unclean and isolated her socially.

chapters.n: She quietly touches the edge of His robe from behind, and the bleeding stops instantly.

f.g: Likely the tassels (fringes) Jewish men wore on the corners of their cloaks.
Stopped flowing.

chapters.n: Jesus asks who touched Him. Peter points out the obvious — everyone is bumping into Him! But Jesus means a different kind of touch: one of faith.

f.g: Greek epistatēs, “chief” or “commander” — a title of respect used only by Luke.

chapters.n: Jesus felt power go out of Him. Healing was not effortless or impersonal; He knew that a specific person had reached out in faith.

f.g: Power (Greek dynamis), not moral goodness.

chapters.n: Realizing she can’t remain hidden, the woman comes forward trembling and tells everyone what happened. Her healing becomes a public testimony.

f.w: declared unto him before all the people
f.g: Her public witness also restored her standing in the community.

chapters.n: Jesus calls her “Daughter” — a word of tenderness and belonging. He affirms her faith and sends her off in peace, healed in body and restored in spirit.

f.g: Greek sōzō, which can mean both “heal” and “save.”

chapters.n: While Jesus is still speaking, terrible news arrives: the girl has died. Don’t bother the Teacher anymore, the messenger says.

f.g: Here Greek didaskalos, “Teacher.”

chapters.n: Jesus immediately reassures Jairus: don’t be afraid, just keep believing. The delay that cost him precious time has not cost him his daughter.
Jesus takes only Peter, James, and John — the same three who later witness the Transfiguration and Gethsemane — along with the parents.
The house is full of mourners. Jesus says she is only sleeping — death, in His hands, is as temporary as sleep.

f.g: Mourned loudly; professional mourners were common at Jewish funerals.

f.w: she is not dead, but sleepeth

chapters.n: The mourners mock Him, certain she is dead. Their scorn sets up the miracle that follows.

f.g: Ridiculed Him.

chapters.n: Jesus clears the room, takes the girl’s hand, and simply tells her to get up.

f.g: Mark preserves His Aramaic words: “Talitha cumi.”

chapters.n: Her spirit returns to her body and she rises immediately. Jesus’ practical instruction to feed her shows His care for ordinary needs, and proves she is truly alive.

f.g: Death is the separation of spirit and body; here the spirit returns.
Food of any kind.

chapters.n: The parents are stunned. Jesus asks them to keep it quiet — perhaps to avoid crowds seeking only spectacle, since His time to be openly proclaimed had not yet come.

f.g: Instructed them firmly.

chapters.n: Jesus gathers the Twelve and gives them both power (the ability) and authority (the right) to act in His name over evil spirits and disease. This is priesthood delegation in action.
Their mission mirrors His own: proclaim God’s kingdom and heal. Teaching and ministering to physical needs go hand in hand.

f.g: Greek apostellō, the root of “apostle” — one who is sent.

chapters.n: They are to travel light and trust God and the hospitality of others for their needs. The lesson is dependence on the Lord rather than on their own provisions.

f.g: Walking sticks.
A traveler’s bag for food and supplies.

chapters.n: Once welcomed into a home, they should stay there rather than shop around for better lodging. Contentment and loyalty to their hosts honors the work.

f.g: Stay.

chapters.n: Where people reject the message, the missionaries are to shake the dust off their feet — a symbolic act showing they have done their part and the responsibility now rests with the hearers.

f.w: shake off the very dust from your feet

chapters.n: The Twelve obey and go out, preaching the gospel and healing in village after village. Jesus’ ministry is multiplied through them.

f.g: Literally “announcing good news.”

chapters.n: News reaches Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. He is troubled because some say John the Baptist, whom he executed, has come back from the dead.

f.g: Ruler of a quarter — Herod Antipas governed Galilee and Perea under Rome after his father Herod the Great died.
Thoroughly puzzled and uneasy.

chapters.n: Others guess Jesus is Elijah returned, or another ancient prophet. Everyone senses He is someone extraordinary, but they cannot yet see who He truly is.

f.g: Greek form of the Hebrew name Elijah.

chapters.n: Herod’s guilty conscience speaks: he knows he killed John. His curiosity to see Jesus is finally satisfied at Jesus’ trial, but without faith.
The apostles return and report. Jesus takes them away to a quiet place near Bethsaida to rest — a reminder that even busy servants need time apart.

f.g: “House of fishing,” a town near where the Jordan enters the north end of the Sea of Galilee; home of Peter, Andrew, and Philip.
A lonely, uninhabited area, not necessarily sand dunes.

chapters.n: The crowds find them anyway. Instead of turning them away, Jesus welcomes them, teaches them, and heals those in need — compassion overriding His own need for rest.

f.g: He welcomed them warmly.

chapters.n: As evening approaches, the Twelve suggest sending the crowd off to find food and lodging. It seems the sensible thing to do in such a remote place.

f.g: Food, provisions.
Find a place to stay.

chapters.n: Jesus surprises them: “You feed them.” They can only count five loaves and two fish. He is teaching them to see what God can do with what little they have.

f.g: Food.

chapters.n: About five thousand men, plus women and children, are present. Jesus organizes them into groups of fifty, bringing order to the miracle.
The disciples follow His instructions and seat the crowd, acting in faith before they see how the food will appear.

f.g: Literally “recline,” the usual posture for a meal.

chapters.n: Jesus looks to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives the food to the disciples to distribute. These same actions will be repeated at the Last Supper, pointing to Him as the Bread of Life.
Everyone eats until satisfied, and twelve baskets of leftovers remain — more than they started with. God’s provision overflows.

f.g: Perhaps one for each apostle; the number twelve also recalls the tribes of Israel.

chapters.n: Luke, who often shows Jesus praying before key moments, places this question right after a time of prayer. Jesus asks what people are saying about Him.
The disciples report the popular opinions: John the Baptist, Elijah, or another prophet. People admire Him but miss His true identity.

f.g: Elijah.

chapters.n: Then Jesus makes it personal: “But who do you say I am?” Peter answers with a testimony: You are the Christ, the Anointed One sent by God.

f.g: Christ (Greek) and Messiah (Hebrew) both mean “Anointed One.”

chapters.n: Jesus tells them firmly not to spread this yet. Many expected a political Messiah, and He needed them first to understand what kind of Messiah He would be.

f.g: Strictly ordered.

chapters.n: Right after Peter’s confession, Jesus reveals that the Messiah must suffer, be rejected by the religious leaders, be killed, and rise on the third day. The Atonement is central to His mission.

f.g: Jesus’ favorite title for Himself; also echoing “Man of Holiness,” a name of God.

chapters.n: Discipleship means setting aside self-will and shouldering one’s own cross — every day. Luke’s word “daily” makes it a continual commitment, not a one-time act.

f.g: JST Matthew 16:26 adds that to take up one’s cross is to deny oneself of all ungodliness and worldly lust.

chapters.n: Here is the great paradox of the gospel: clutching our life for ourselves loses it, while giving it to Christ is how we truly find and keep it.

f.w: lose his life for my sake

chapters.n: Gaining everything the world offers is worthless if we lose our own souls in the process. Nothing is worth trading for eternal life.

f.g: Profited, benefited.

chapters.n: Anyone embarrassed to stand with Jesus and His teachings now will find Him unwilling to claim them when He returns in glory with His Father and the angels.
Jesus promises that some there will see God’s kingdom before they die. The Transfiguration, which follows immediately, is one fulfillment; Latter-day Saints also understand John’s promised tarrying.
About a week later Jesus takes Peter, John, and James up a mountain to pray. Mountains in scripture are often places of revelation.

f.g: Traditionally Mount Tabor; many scholars favor Mount Hermon near Caesarea Philippi.

chapters.n: While praying, Jesus is transfigured: His face changes and His clothes shine dazzling white, revealing the glory He had with the Father.

f.g: Gleaming, flashing like lightning.

f.w: the fashion of his countenance was altered

chapters.n: Moses and Elijah appear and talk with Him. Moses represents the law and Elijah the prophets — both bearing witness of Christ. Latter-day revelation teaches they also conferred priesthood keys on Peter, James, and John.
Only Luke records their topic: Jesus’ coming “decease” in Jerusalem. The glorious vision centers on His suffering and death.

f.g: Greek exodos, “departure” — echoing Israel’s Exodus; Jesus’ death would lead a new deliverance.

chapters.n: The three apostles were weighed down with sleep, but they fully awoke and saw His glory and the two heavenly visitors.
As Moses and Elijah begin to leave, Peter blurts out an offer to build three shelters, wanting to prolong the moment. Luke kindly notes he didn’t really know what he was saying.

f.g: Booths or tents, like those used at the Feast of Tabernacles.

chapters.n: A cloud overshadows them, like the cloud of God’s presence that led Israel and filled the tabernacle. The disciples are filled with awe as they enter it.
The Father speaks from the cloud, testifying that Jesus is His Son and commanding them to listen to Him — the Prophet greater than Moses.

f.w: This is my beloved Son: hear him

chapters.n: Suddenly only Jesus remains. The three keep what they saw to themselves, as Jesus had asked, until after the Resurrection.

f.g: Kept it secret.

chapters.n: The next day, coming down from the mountain, they meet a large crowd. Glory on the mountain gives way to human need in the valley.

f.g: The mountain of the Transfiguration.

chapters.n: A father shouts out a plea for his only child. Luke often notes when a child is an only child, highlighting a parent’s desperation.
The boy suffers violent seizures caused by an evil spirit: screaming, convulsing, foaming at the mouth, and being badly bruised.

f.g: Battering him severely; “hardly” means scarcely or with difficulty does it leave him.

chapters.n: The father reports that the disciples tried to cast it out but failed. Their earlier success had not yet taught them full dependence on God.
Jesus expresses grief at the unbelief around Him — among the crowd and even His disciples — then asks for the boy to be brought.

f.g: Twisted, turned away from what is right.
Put up with you.

chapters.n: Even as the boy approaches, the spirit throws him into a convulsion. Jesus rebukes it, heals the child, and gives him back to his father — a tender, restoring act.

f.g: Tore at him, threw him into convulsions.

chapters.n: Everyone marvels at God’s power. But amid the excitement, Jesus turns His disciples’ attention to something harder to accept.

f.g: Greek megaleiotēs, majesty or greatness.

chapters.n: He tells them to let these words sink in: He will be handed over to men. Popularity would not last; the cross was coming.

f.g: Handed over or betrayed.

chapters.n: They could not grasp it — the idea of a suffering Messiah did not fit their expectations — and they were afraid to ask Him about it.
Instead of understanding His humility, the disciples begin arguing about which of them is greatest — a painful contrast to His talk of suffering.

f.g: A dispute or debate.

chapters.n: Knowing their thoughts, Jesus places a little child next to Himself as a living lesson.

f.g: Next to Himself — a place of honor.

chapters.n: Welcoming the lowly — like a child, who had no status in that culture — is welcoming Christ and the Father. In His kingdom, greatness is measured by humility.

f.w: he that is least among you all, the same shall be great

chapters.n: John reports that they stopped someone casting out devils in Jesus’ name because he wasn’t part of their group.

f.g: Tried to stop.

chapters.n: Jesus tells them not to stop such people. Those doing good in His name are allies, not rivals. He rebukes a narrow, competitive spirit.

f.w: he that is not against us is for us

chapters.n: This marks a turning point in Luke. Knowing His time to be “received up” is near, Jesus resolutely heads for Jerusalem and the cross. Much of Luke 9–19 takes place on this journey.

f.g: Taken up — referring to His death, resurrection, and ascension.

chapters.n: He sends messengers ahead to arrange lodging in a Samaritan village along the way.

f.g: People of mixed Israelite heritage in central Palestine; Jews and Samaritans disagreed sharply over where to worship.
