chapters.n: The Samaritans refuse to host Him because He is heading to Jerusalem, the rival worship center to their own Mount Gerizim.

f.w: his face was as though he would go to Jerusalem
f.g: He was clearly traveling toward Jerusalem.

chapters.n: James and John offer to call down fire like Elijah did. Their zeal is real, but their spirit is wrong — perhaps one reason Jesus called them “sons of thunder.”
Jesus turns and rebukes them. They don’t yet understand the spirit of His gospel, which is love, not vengeance.

f.w: Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of
f.g: Not in all ancient manuscripts, but fits Jesus’ teaching.

chapters.n: The Son of Man came to save lives, not destroy them. They simply move on to another village — answering rejection with patience.

f.w: not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them

chapters.n: On the road, a man enthusiastically promises to follow Jesus anywhere.

f.g: Wherever.

chapters.n: Jesus warns him to count the cost: even animals have homes, but He has none. Following Him means giving up comfort and security.

f.w: the Son of man hath not where to lay his head

chapters.n: Jesus invites another man, who asks to first bury his father. In that culture this might mean waiting until his father died, possibly years away.

f.g: Allow me.

chapters.n: Jesus’ startling answer: let the spiritually dead take care of such matters. The call to preach God’s kingdom takes priority over every other duty.

f.w: Let the dead bury their dead
f.g: Those spiritually dead can handle ordinary affairs; the disciple has a living work to do.

chapters.n: A third person wants to say goodbye at home first. Elijah allowed Elisha this, but Jesus’ call is even more urgent.
A farmer who keeps looking backward while plowing cuts a crooked furrow. A disciple whose heart keeps drifting back to the old life isn’t ready for the kingdom.

f.g: Plow; a light plow guided with one hand required forward focus.

chapters.n: Beyond the Twelve, Jesus appoints seventy more and sends them in pairs ahead of Him to prepare towns for His visit. Only Luke records this mission. The Church today still has quorums of the Seventy who serve under the Twelve.

f.g: Some early manuscripts read seventy-two. The number recalls the seventy elders who helped Moses.

chapters.n: There are many people ready to receive the gospel but few workers to gather them. Jesus asks the disciples to pray for more laborers — and then sends them as an answer to that very prayer.
They go out vulnerable, like lambs surrounded by wolves. Their safety will come from God, not from their own strength.
No money bag, no supply sack, no extra sandals — and no long roadside greetings. The mission is urgent, and they must rely fully on the Lord.

f.w: salute no man by the way
f.g: Eastern greetings could involve lengthy ceremonies; they were not to be delayed by social formalities.
A traveler’s food bag.

chapters.n: Their first words on entering a home are to be a blessing of peace — the common Jewish greeting “Shalom,” now carrying the peace of the gospel.
If someone receptive lives there, the blessing of peace will rest on that home. If not, the blessing comes back to the missionaries — nothing is wasted.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for a person of peace, someone open to it.

chapters.n: They are to stay in the same house and accept whatever food is offered. Those who labor in the Lord’s work may rightly receive support from those they serve.

f.w: the labourer is worthy of his hire
Go not from house to house
f.g: Don’t move around seeking better accommodations.

chapters.n: In welcoming towns, they should gratefully eat what is served — without fussing over food customs.

f.w: eat such things as are set before you

chapters.n: They are to heal the sick and announce that God’s kingdom has drawn near. Healing shows the kingdom’s power; preaching explains it.

f.g: Near.

chapters.n: If a town refuses them, they are to go out into its streets and make a public declaration.
Wiping off the town’s dust is a solemn witness that they bear no responsibility for the town’s choice. Yet even in rejection, the message stands: the kingdom came near.

f.g: Clings, sticks.

chapters.n: Sodom was notorious for wickedness, yet it never had the chance these towns had. Those who reject greater light carry greater accountability.

f.g: More bearable.

chapters.n: Jesus mourns over Galilean towns where He had done many miracles. Even the pagan cities of Tyre and Sidon would have repented long ago had they seen what these towns saw.

f.g: A town just north of Capernaum.
Rough goat-hair clothing and ashes on the head — signs of grief and repentance.

chapters.n: On Judgment Day, these Gentile cities will fare better than the towns that saw Jesus’ works and still refused Him.

f.g: Ancient Phoenician seaports on the Mediterranean coast north of Galilee.

chapters.n: Capernaum, Jesus’ home base, had been lifted up by His presence — yet in its pride it would be brought down. Its ruins today stand as a quiet witness.

f.g: Greek hadēs, the world of departed spirits; here the depths, the opposite of heaven.

chapters.n: To hear Christ’s authorized servants is to hear Christ, and to reject them is to reject Him and His Father. The authority of the messenger comes from the One who sends.

f.w: He that heareth you heareth me

chapters.n: The seventy return thrilled: even evil spirits obeyed them in Jesus’ name.
Jesus sees their success as part of Satan’s defeat. Satan was cast out of heaven long ago, and now his power on earth is being broken.

f.w: I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven

chapters.n: Jesus gives them authority over every power of the enemy — symbolized by snakes and scorpions. Nothing will be able to defeat them spiritually.
Still, power over spirits is not the true reason for joy. The greater joy is having one’s name recorded in heaven — belonging to God forever.

f.w: your names are written in heaven

chapters.n: Jesus overflows with joy and thanks the Father that heavenly truths have been revealed to the humble and childlike, while those proud of their learning miss them.

f.g: Little children — here the humble and teachable.

f.w: hid these things from the wise and prudent

chapters.n: The Father has given all things to the Son. Only the Father fully knows the Son, and only the Son fully knows the Father — and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.

f.w: he to whom the Son will reveal him

chapters.n: Privately, Jesus tells His disciples how blessed they are to witness these things.

f.w: Blessed are the eyes which see

chapters.n: Prophets and kings of old longed to see the Messiah’s day, but only saw it from afar. The disciples are living what generations looked forward to.

f.w: many prophets and kings have desired to see

chapters.n: An expert in the law of Moses tests Jesus with the most important question anyone can ask: how do I gain eternal life?

f.g: Not a courtroom attorney but a scholar of the law of Moses.
Tested.

chapters.n: Jesus turns the question back: You know the law — what does it say? How do you read it?

f.g: How do you interpret it?

chapters.n: The lawyer answers well, combining two commandments: love God completely (from Deuteronomy) and love your neighbor as yourself (from Leviticus).

f.w: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God

chapters.n: Jesus agrees: correct answer. Now live it, and you will have life. Knowing isn’t enough — doing is what matters.

f.w: this do, and thou shalt live

chapters.n: Wanting to justify himself, the lawyer looks for a limit: exactly who counts as my neighbor? He hopes to narrow his obligation.

f.g: Make himself look right.

chapters.n: Jesus tells a story. The steep road from Jerusalem down to Jericho dropped about 3,000 feet through rocky, lonely country and was known for bandits. A traveler is robbed, beaten, and left for dead.

f.w: went down from Jerusalem to Jericho
f.g: About 17 miles, descending from about 2,500 feet above sea level to about 800 feet below.
Clothing.

chapters.n: A priest comes by — someone who served at the temple. He sees the man and deliberately crosses to the other side. Perhaps he feared ritual defilement from a possible corpse, or simply didn’t want the trouble.

f.w: passed by on the other side

chapters.n: A Levite, a temple assistant, does the same — looking at the man, then passing by. Religious standing did not produce compassion.

f.g: A member of the tribe of Levi who assisted the priests in temple service.

chapters.n: The hero is a Samaritan — someone Jews of that day despised. Moved with compassion, he stops. Jesus deliberately makes the outsider the example.

f.g: Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility; the lawyer would never expect him to be the hero.

chapters.n: He treats the wounds with oil to soothe and wine to disinfect, puts the man on his own animal, takes him to an inn, and cares for him through the night. Many early Christians saw Christ Himself in this rescuer.

f.g: Common first-aid of the day: olive oil soothed; wine cleansed.
His pack animal, likely a donkey.

chapters.n: The next day he pays the innkeeper two denarii — about two days’ wages — and promises to cover anything more when he returns. His mercy is generous and lasting.

f.g: Two denarii; a denarius was a typical day’s wage for a laborer.

f.w: when I come again, I will repay thee
f.g: Many readers see a hint of Christ’s promised return.

chapters.n: Jesus flips the lawyer’s question. Not “who is my neighbor?” but “who acted as a neighbor?” The question is not whom we must love, but whether we will love.

f.g: Being a neighbor is an action, not a category.

chapters.n: The lawyer can’t bring himself to say “the Samaritan,” but he gives the right answer: the one who showed mercy. Jesus’ command is simple: go and do the same.
Jesus enters a village — John tells us it was Bethany near Jerusalem — and Martha welcomes Him into her home.
Her sister Mary sits at Jesus’ feet listening to Him — the posture of a disciple. Remarkably, Jesus welcomes a woman as a student of His teaching.

f.g: The traditional position of a student before a rabbi.

chapters.n: Martha is overwhelmed by all the work of hosting and asks Jesus to tell Mary to help. Her service is good, but she has become anxious and resentful.

f.g: Distracted, pulled in many directions.

chapters.n: Jesus speaks to her tenderly, repeating her name. He sees that she is anxious and upset about so many things.

f.g: Full of care — anxious, worried.

chapters.n: Only one thing is truly necessary: drawing near to Him. Mary has chosen the best part, and Jesus will not take it from her. Service matters, but never at the cost of being with the Lord.

f.g: The best portion, as in the choice share of a meal.

chapters.n: Watching Jesus pray makes the disciples want to learn how. Rabbis often gave their followers a characteristic prayer, as John the Baptist had done, so one disciple asks Jesus for His.
Jesus begins with God: He is our Father, His name is holy, and we long for His kingdom and will to prevail on earth as in heaven. Prayer starts by aligning our desires with His.

f.g: Honored as holy.

chapters.n: We ask for what we need today — and then again tomorrow. Like manna in the wilderness, daily dependence keeps us close to God.
We seek forgiveness while forgiving others, and we plead for protection from trial and evil. Receiving mercy and extending it go together.

f.g: Owing us — anyone who has wronged us.
JST Matthew 6:14 reads “suffer us not to be led into temptation.”

chapters.n: Jesus tells a story: imagine going to a friend’s house at midnight to borrow three loaves of bread.

f.g: Small flat loaves — enough for a meal for one guest.

chapters.n: An unexpected traveler has arrived, and in that culture failing to feed a guest was shameful. The need is real and urgent.

f.g: Serve him as a meal.

chapters.n: The friend inside complains: the door is barred and the whole family is asleep in one room. Getting up would wake everyone.

f.g: Village doors were secured with a heavy bar at night.

chapters.n: Even if friendship isn’t enough, the persistent asking will get him out of bed. If a reluctant neighbor responds to persistence, how much more will a loving God respond?

f.g: Persistence; shameless boldness in asking.

chapters.n: Jesus gives three invitations with three promises: ask and receive, seek and find, knock and the door opens. These words echo throughout scripture and helped launch the Restoration.

f.w: Ask, and it shall be given you

chapters.n: The promise is universal: everyone who asks receives. God’s answers may differ from what we expect, but He always hears and responds.
No loving father would hand his hungry son a stone that looks like bread, or a snake instead of a fish.

f.g: Snake.

chapters.n: Nor would he give a scorpion — perhaps a curled-up one that looks like an egg. Earthly parents don’t trick their children.

f.g: Some scorpions in the region are pale and, when curled, could resemble an egg.

chapters.n: If imperfect human parents give good gifts, our Heavenly Father will surely give His greatest gift — the Holy Ghost — to those who ask. Luke emphasizes the Spirit throughout his Gospel and Acts.

f.w: give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him

chapters.n: Jesus casts out a spirit that had made a man unable to speak. When it leaves, the man talks, and the crowd is amazed.

f.g: Unable to speak (not lacking intelligence).

chapters.n: Some critics can’t deny the miracle, so they attack its source, claiming Jesus works by the power of the prince of devils.

f.g: Possibly “lord of the flies” or “lord of the dwelling,” a name for Satan.

chapters.n: Others test Him by demanding a sign from heaven — as if the miracle just performed weren’t enough.

f.g: Testing Him.

chapters.n: Jesus, knowing their thoughts, answers with common sense: any kingdom or household fighting itself will fall apart.

f.g: Ruin.

chapters.n: If Satan were casting out his own servants, he’d be destroying his own kingdom. Their accusation makes no sense.

f.g: A rhetorical question — it couldn’t.

chapters.n: Some Jewish exorcists also cast out spirits. If the critics accept those, their own followers will testify against the double standard.

f.g: Your followers or disciples.

chapters.n: If Jesus is acting by God’s power, then God’s kingdom has arrived among them. “The finger of God” recalls the miracles in Egypt that even Pharaoh’s magicians recognized.
Picture a strong, armed man guarding his house; his possessions seem safe. Satan is that strong man, holding people captive.

f.g: A courtyard or fortified house.

chapters.n: But someone stronger comes, defeats him, strips his armor, and divides the plunder. Christ is the Stronger One who frees Satan’s captives.

f.g: Plunder taken in battle.

chapters.n: There is no neutral ground. Those not actively gathering with Christ are, in effect, scattering.

f.w: He that is not with me is against me

chapters.n: A spirit cast out wanders through barren places looking for rest, finds none, and decides to return to the person it left.

f.g: Desert regions, thought to be haunts of evil spirits.

chapters.n: It finds the house cleaned and decorated — but empty. Removing evil isn’t enough; the heart must be filled with something good.

f.g: Decorated, put in order.

chapters.n: It brings seven worse spirits, and the person ends up worse off than before. Reformation without filling the life with God leaves us vulnerable.

f.w: the last state of that man is worse than the first

chapters.n: A woman in the crowd calls out a blessing on Jesus’ mother — a typical way of praising a remarkable son.

f.g: Breasts.

chapters.n: Jesus doesn’t deny His mother’s blessedness, but points to something even greater and available to everyone: hearing God’s word and keeping it.

f.g: Yes — but even more.

f.w: hear the word of God, and keep it

chapters.n: As crowds grow, Jesus rebukes the demand for signs. The only sign they’ll receive is the sign of Jonah.

f.g: Greek form of the name Jonah.

chapters.n: Jonah himself — a prophet who came back as if from death — was a sign to Nineveh. Jesus, rising from the dead, will be the sign to His generation.

f.g: People of Nineveh, capital of Assyria.

chapters.n: The Queen of Sheba traveled a great distance to hear Solomon’s wisdom. Someone far greater than Solomon is here, yet many will not cross the street to hear Him.

f.g: The Queen of Sheba, probably from southern Arabia.

chapters.n: Nineveh repented at Jonah’s brief message. These pagans will stand as witnesses against a generation that ignored a far greater prophet.

f.g: Nineveh.

f.w: a greater than Jonas is here

chapters.n: Light is meant to be displayed, not hidden under a basket. Jesus is that light, openly offered to all.

f.g: A basket or container for measuring grain.

chapters.n: The eye is like a window letting light into the body. A “single” eye — focused wholly on God — fills the whole person with light; a corrupt eye lets in darkness.

f.g: Undivided, sincere, focused.

chapters.n: Be careful that what you think is light inside you isn’t actually darkness. Self-deception is a real danger.

f.g: Be careful.

chapters.n: When a person is completely filled with light, with no dark corners, they shine as brightly as a lamp. This is the goal of discipleship.
A Pharisee invites Jesus to a meal, and He accepts. Luke often shows Jesus eating with all kinds of people, including His critics.

f.g: Reclined at the table for a meal.

chapters.n: The host is shocked that Jesus skips the ceremonial hand-washing — not a hygiene rule but a religious tradition added to the law.

f.g: Ritual washing required by Pharisaic tradition, not by the law of Moses.

chapters.n: Jesus uses dishes as a metaphor: the Pharisees scrub the outside of cups but leave the inside filthy — clean in appearance, greedy and wicked within.

f.g: Greed, plunder.
A dish or plate.

chapters.n: God made both the outside and the inside of a person. How foolish to care only for appearances when He sees the heart.

f.g: Senseless ones — a sharp but not hateful rebuke.

chapters.n: Instead, give generously from the heart. Inner generosity cleanses far more than outward washing.

f.g: Gifts to the poor.

chapters.n: They carefully tithe even tiny garden herbs, but neglect justice and love for God. Jesus doesn’t dismiss tithing — He says do both, but don’t lose the weightier matters.

f.g: A bitter herb used for seasoning and medicine.
Give a tenth.

chapters.n: They crave the best seats and public honor. Their religion has become a stage for status.

f.g: The front seats facing the congregation, reserved for honored people.

chapters.n: Touching a grave made a Jew ritually unclean. The hypocrites are like unmarked graves — people are defiled by them without even knowing it.

f.g: Unmarked graves; tombs were usually whitewashed so people could avoid them.

chapters.n: A legal scholar protests that Jesus is insulting them too.

f.g: Insult, rebuke.

chapters.n: Jesus answers: yes, you too. Experts pile heavy rules on people but won’t lift a finger to help them carry the load.

f.g: Load down.

chapters.n: They honor dead prophets by building monuments, while their ancestors killed those prophets — and they’re about to do the same to the living ones.

f.g: Tombs.

chapters.n: By building the tombs, they are finishing what their fathers began — the fathers killed, the sons bury. They are approving their ancestors’ deeds.

f.g: Approve of, consent to.

chapters.n: God’s wisdom foresaw that He would send prophets and apostles, and that some would be killed and persecuted.

f.g: Perhaps referring to God speaking in His wisdom; Matthew presents these as Jesus’ own words.

chapters.n: The guilt of all the righteous blood shed throughout history will be held against this generation, which is rejecting the greatest Prophet of all.

f.g: Held accountable, demanded in payment.

chapters.n: From Abel, the first murder in Genesis, to Zechariah, the last in the Hebrew Bible’s order of books (2 Chronicles) — the whole span of scripture’s martyrs.
These experts hold the key to understanding scripture but neither enter themselves nor let others in. The JST says the key they took away was “the fulness of the scriptures.”

f.g: JST Luke 11:53: “the key of knowledge, the fulness of the scriptures.”

chapters.n: Furious, the scribes and Pharisees start grilling Jesus aggressively, firing questions to provoke Him.

f.g: Intensely, with hostility.

chapters.n: They lie in wait, hoping to trap Him into saying something they could use against Him. The opposition that leads to the cross is growing.
With thousands pressing in so tightly they trample one another, Jesus first warns His disciples about hypocrisy. Like yeast in dough, a little pretense quietly spreads through everything.

f.g: Yeast or fermented dough; in scripture often a symbol of corrupting influence.
Greek hypokrisis, originally an actor playing a part behind a mask.

chapters.n: Pretending won’t work forever. Everything hidden will eventually be exposed, so it is better to be genuine now.

f.w: nothing covered, that shall not be revealed

chapters.n: Words whispered privately will one day be shouted from the rooftops. Flat roofs were places where public announcements could be made.

f.g: Inner rooms, private chambers.
Flat roofs used for living space and for making announcements.

chapters.n: Calling His disciples “friends,” Jesus tells them not to fear persecutors. The worst they can do is kill the body, which is not the end of a person.
The One to reverently fear is God, who holds eternal destiny in His hands. Holy fear of God drives out fear of people.

f.g: Greek geenna (Gehenna), named for the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a symbol of final judgment.

chapters.n: Sparrows were so cheap that you got five for two pennies — one was thrown in free. Yet God remembers each one.

f.g: Small Roman copper coins (assarion), each worth a fraction of a day’s wage.

f.w: not one of them is forgotten before God

chapters.n: God knows us down to the number of hairs on our heads. If He cares for sparrows, how much more does He value each of His children?

f.w: the very hairs of your head are all numbered

chapters.n: Those who openly acknowledge Christ before others will be acknowledged by Him before God’s angels.
Those who deny Him will be denied. Our loyalty to Christ now shapes how He will stand with us later.
Words spoken against the Son of Man can be forgiven, but willfully rejecting the witness of the Holy Ghost after receiving it cannot. Latter-day revelation explains this unpardonable sin.
When disciples are hauled before religious or civil authorities, they shouldn’t worry in advance about defending themselves.

f.g: Civil officials and judges.
Don’t be anxious.

chapters.n: The Holy Ghost will give them the right words at the right moment. This promise is repeated to missionaries in the latter days.

f.w: the Holy Ghost shall teach you in the same hour

chapters.n: Someone in the crowd interrupts, asking Jesus to settle a family dispute over inheritance. Rabbis were often asked to rule on such matters.

f.g: Under the law, an elder brother received a double share.

chapters.n: Jesus declines to act as an arbiter. His mission is not to divide property but to address the heart.

f.g: One who divides an estate — an arbitrator.

chapters.n: He warns against every form of greed. Life isn’t measured by how much we own.

f.g: Greed, the craving for more.

f.w: abundance of the things which he possesseth

chapters.n: Jesus tells a parable about a rich man whose land produced a huge harvest. The wealth itself isn’t the problem — it’s what he does with it.

f.g: Produced a bumper crop.

chapters.n: He talks only to himself. His problem: too much stuff and not enough room. He never thinks of God or of the hungry.

f.g: Store.

chapters.n: His solution is bigger barns. Notice how many times he says “I” and “my” — his world revolves around himself.

f.g: Count the possessives: my fruits, my barns, my goods, my soul.

chapters.n: He plans an easy life for years ahead: eat, drink, and enjoy. He assumes he controls his future.
God calls him a fool: his life ends tonight. All his hoarded wealth will go to someone else. He prepared for everything except eternity.

f.g: In Hebrew thought, a fool is one who lives as if there is no God.

f.w: this night thy soul shall be required of thee

chapters.n: This is the fate of everyone who hoards for themselves but isn’t rich in the things that matter to God — faith, love, generosity.
Turning to His disciples, Jesus tells them not to be consumed with anxiety over food and clothing.

f.g: Don’t worry anxiously — not a ban on planning.

chapters.n: Life is bigger than food, and the body is more than its clothing. God, who gave the greater gifts, will surely provide the lesser.

f.g: Food.
Clothing.

chapters.n: Ravens don’t farm or store up food, yet God feeds them. Ravens were unclean birds under the law — if God feeds even them, how much more His children!
Worry can’t add a single moment to your life — or an inch to your height. It accomplishes nothing.

f.g: About 18 inches; here possibly a measure of lifespan rather than height.

chapters.n: If worry can’t even do something so small, why let it control the bigger things of life?

f.g: Worry.

chapters.n: Wildflowers don’t labor or weave cloth, yet they are dressed more beautifully than King Solomon at his most splendid.

f.g: Probably the wildflowers that blanket Galilean hills in spring.

chapters.n: If God clothes the grass, which lasts only a day before being burned as fuel, He will certainly take care of you. Jesus gently chides their small faith.

f.g: Dried grass was used to heat clay ovens.

chapters.n: Don’t make food and drink your main pursuit, and don’t be anxious or unsettled about them.

f.g: Anxious, tossed back and forth like a ship.

chapters.n: These are the things the whole world chases after. Your Father already knows what you need.

f.g: The Gentiles — those who don’t know God.

chapters.n: Make God’s kingdom your priority, and He will provide what you need along the way.

f.w: seek ye the kingdom of God

chapters.n: One of the tenderest verses in scripture: do not fear, little flock. It delights the Father to give you His kingdom.

f.g: Joyful will, delight.

chapters.n: Turn earthly wealth into heavenly treasure by giving to those in need. Heaven’s “purses” never wear out, and nothing stored there can be stolen or ruined.

f.g: Money purses that don’t wear out.
Gifts to the poor.

chapters.n: Our hearts follow our treasure. What we invest in reveals and shapes what we love.
Be dressed and ready with lamps lit. Long robes were tucked into the belt for active work; lamps were kept burning for a night arrival.

f.w: Let your loins be girded about
f.g: Tuck up your robe — be ready for action.

chapters.n: Be like servants waiting up for their master to return from a wedding feast, ready to open the door the moment he knocks.

f.g: Wedding feasts could last days, so the return time was uncertain.

chapters.n: In an astonishing reversal, the master himself puts on an apron and serves the faithful servants. This is how Christ treats those who wait for Him.
Even if he comes in the middle of the night or close to dawn, the servants found ready will be blessed.

f.g: The Jews divided the night into three watches; the second and third covered roughly 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.

chapters.n: A homeowner who knew when a burglar was coming would stay alert and protect his house.

f.g: Master of the household.
Literally “dug through” — houses with mud-brick walls could be broken into by digging.

chapters.n: So be ready always, because Christ will return when people least expect it.

f.w: the Son of man cometh at an hour when ye think not

chapters.n: Peter asks whether this teaching is for the apostles specifically or for everyone.
Jesus answers with a question about the faithful steward — a trusted servant put in charge of feeding the household on time. Leaders have special responsibility.

f.g: A household manager entrusted with another’s property.
At the proper time.

chapters.n: That servant will be blessed when the master returns and finds him faithfully at work.

f.g: Doing his duty.

chapters.n: The faithful servant will be given charge of everything the master owns — faithfulness in small things leads to greater trust.

f.w: ruler over all that he hath

chapters.n: But if the servant assumes the master won’t be back soon and starts abusing others and partying, he betrays his trust.
The master will arrive unexpectedly and punish him severely, placing him among the unfaithful.

f.g: Cut him in pieces — a vivid image of severe judgment.

chapters.n: A servant who knew what his master wanted and deliberately ignored it will receive heavy punishment. Knowledge increases accountability.

f.g: Lashes from a whip.

chapters.n: Those who sinned in ignorance receive lighter judgment. The principle: the more we are given, the more is expected of us.

f.w: unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required

chapters.n: Jesus came to kindle a fire on the earth — a refining, purifying fire of the gospel and the Spirit. He longs to see it blazing.
Before that, He must pass through a “baptism” of suffering — His Atonement and death. He feels the weight of it pressing on Him until it is finished.

f.w: a baptism to be baptized with

f.g: Distressed, pressed, constrained.

chapters.n: Jesus brings ultimate peace, but in the short term His message will divide people — some accepting, others rejecting.
Even within a single household, people will take sides over Him.

f.g: A family of five split by different responses to Christ.

chapters.n: These words echo Micah’s prophecy of family conflict. Choosing Christ can strain even the closest relationships.

f.w: The father shall be divided against the son

chapters.n: Turning to the crowd, Jesus notes how well they read the weather: clouds from the Mediterranean in the west mean rain.

f.g: The Mediterranean Sea lies west of Israel.

chapters.n: A south wind from the desert brings scorching heat. They read these signs perfectly.

f.g: Wind from the Negev and Arabian deserts.

chapters.n: They can forecast weather but fail to recognize the most important sign of all — that the Messiah is among them.
Why can’t they judge for themselves what is right? They have enough evidence to decide.

f.g: On your own, without needing a sign.

chapters.n: If you are being taken to court, settle with your opponent on the way before the judge hands you over to be imprisoned. Make peace with God now, before judgment comes.

f.g: Drag.
Make every effort.

chapters.n: Once in prison, you won’t leave until the last tiny coin is paid. Better to reconcile now while there is time — repentance is urgent.

f.g: Greek lepton, the smallest copper coin.

chapters.n: Some people report a recent atrocity: Pilate had killed Galileans while they were offering sacrifices, mixing their blood with that of their animals. History doesn’t otherwise record this incident, but it fits Pilate’s known brutality.

f.g: Pontius Pilate, Roman governor of Judea about AD 26–36.
Killed them at the temple while they worshipped.

chapters.n: Many assumed disaster was punishment for special sin. Jesus challenges that idea: were these victims worse sinners than everyone else?
No, He says — but everyone needs to repent. Rather than speculating about others’ sins, look to your own heart.

f.g: Be destroyed — both physically and spiritually.

chapters.n: Jesus adds an accident: a tower near the Pool of Siloam collapsed, killing eighteen. Were they guiltier than everyone else in Jerusalem?

f.g: A district and pool at the southern end of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Again, no. Tragedies don’t sort the guilty from the innocent. The real lesson: all need repentance, and life is uncertain.

f.g: Some see a foreshadowing of Jerusalem’s destruction in AD 70.

chapters.n: A parable: a vineyard owner keeps finding no fruit on his fig tree. Fig trees were sometimes planted in vineyards. Israel is often pictured as a fig tree or vine.
After three years of coming up empty, he orders it cut down — why let it drain the soil? Some see a hint of Jesus’ three years of ministry to His people.

f.g: The gardener who cares for the vines.
Uses up, takes up space uselessly.

chapters.n: The gardener pleads for one more year. He will dig around it and fertilize it. This pictures Christ’s patient intercession and extra care for us.

f.g: Fertilize it with manure.

f.w: let it alone this year also

chapters.n: If it bears fruit, good. If not, it will be cut down. Mercy is generous but not endless — there is a time to repent.

f.w: if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down

chapters.n: This is the last time Luke shows Jesus teaching in a synagogue. He uses the Sabbath to bring rest and healing.

f.g: The seventh day, Saturday — a day of rest and worship.

chapters.n: A woman has been bent double for eighteen years, unable to stand upright. Luke describes it as a spirit causing her infirmity.

f.g: A disabling condition linked to an evil influence.
Bent over.

chapters.n: Jesus notices her and calls her forward, announcing her freedom before she even asks. He sees those whom others overlook.

f.g: You are set free.

chapters.n: He lays His hands on her, and she instantly stands upright and praises God. Eighteen years of bondage end in a moment.
The synagogue ruler is indignant. Afraid to confront Jesus directly, he scolds the crowd: come to be healed on the six workdays, not on the Sabbath.

f.w: six days in which men ought to work

chapters.n: Jesus calls this hypocrisy. They untie their own animals to water them on the Sabbath. Compassion for livestock is allowed — why not for people?

f.g: Donkey.
Animal pen or manger.

chapters.n: She is a daughter of Abraham — part of God’s covenant people — and Satan has bound her for eighteen years. What day could be better for her release than the day of rest?

f.g: A rare phrase honoring her as an heir of the covenant.

chapters.n: His opponents are put to shame, while ordinary people rejoice at all the wonderful things He is doing.

f.g: Opponents.

chapters.n: Jesus asks what God’s kingdom can be compared to. He uses simple images to describe something vast.

f.g: Compare.

chapters.n: The kingdom begins as small as a mustard seed but grows into a large plant where birds nest. From a few disciples, the Church would spread across the earth.

f.g: Grew.

chapters.n: He offers a second image of the kingdom’s growth.

f.g: Compare.

chapters.n: A woman works a little yeast into a large batch of flour until the whole batch rises. The gospel works quietly from within until it transforms everything.

f.g: About 40 pounds of flour — enough bread for a large gathering.

chapters.n: Luke reminds us that Jesus is steadily traveling toward Jerusalem, teaching as He goes.
Someone asks a speculative question: will only a few be saved? Jesus turns it into a personal challenge.

f.w: are there few that be saved?

chapters.n: Instead of giving a number, He urges: make every effort to enter through the narrow door. Many will want in but won’t be able to.

f.g: Greek agōnizomai, to struggle or agonize, as an athlete competes.
Narrow door.

chapters.n: Once the owner has shut the door, those outside will knock and plead, but he will say he doesn’t know them. There comes a point when it is too late.
They protest that they ate with Him and heard Him teach in their streets. Being near Jesus is not the same as following Him.

f.w: We have eaten and drunk in thy presence

chapters.n: He repeats that He does not know them and sends them away as doers of evil. Familiarity without obedience saves no one.
They will weep in anguish when they see the patriarchs and prophets inside God’s kingdom while they themselves are cast out.

f.g: Grinding teeth — an image of bitter regret and anguish.

chapters.n: People from every direction — Gentiles from all nations — will come and sit at God’s great feast.

f.w: from the east, and from the west

chapters.n: Some who seem last now will be first, and some who seem first will be last. God’s judgments often overturn human expectations.
Some Pharisees warn Jesus to flee because Herod Antipas wants to kill Him. Whether friendly or trying to scare Him off, they urge Him to leave.

f.g: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea.

chapters.n: Jesus calls Herod a “fox” — sly and destructive. Herod cannot stop Him; He will finish His work on His own schedule and reach His goal.

f.g: In Jewish idiom a fox could suggest craftiness or insignificance.
Brought to completion — His mission fulfilled.

chapters.n: He must continue His journey, for a prophet is killed in Jerusalem, not elsewhere. His words are full of sorrowful irony.

f.w: a prophet perish out of Jerusalem
f.g: It would be unfitting for a prophet to die anywhere but Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Jesus grieves over Jerusalem. Like a mother hen sheltering her chicks, He longed to gather and protect its people, but they refused. Christ uses this same image to the Nephites.

f.w: as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings

chapters.n: Their “house” — likely the temple and city — will be left desolate. They will not see Him again until they welcome Him with the words of Psalm 118, both at His triumphal entry and ultimately at His Second Coming.

f.w: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord

f.g: Abandoned, empty.

chapters.n: A leading Pharisee invites Jesus for a Sabbath meal, but the guests are watching Him closely, looking for something to criticize.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for sharing a meal.

chapters.n: A man suffering from dropsy is right in front of Him — perhaps placed there as a test.

f.g: Edema — painful swelling from fluid buildup, often a sign of serious illness.

chapters.n: Jesus asks the experts directly: does the law allow healing on the Sabbath?

f.g: Permitted by the law of Moses.

chapters.n: They stay silent. Jesus takes hold of the man, heals him, and sends him on his way.

f.g: Said nothing.

chapters.n: He asks: if your son or ox fell into a well on the Sabbath, wouldn’t you rescue it right away? Mercy belongs on the Sabbath.

f.g: Some ancient manuscripts read “a son or an ox.”
Immediately.

chapters.n: They have no answer. The point is unanswerable: the Sabbath is for doing good.
Jesus notices guests jockeying for the best places near the host, and He tells a parable about it.

f.g: The places of honor at the table (not separate rooms).
Invited.

chapters.n: At a wedding feast, don’t grab the seat of highest honor. A more distinguished guest might arrive.

f.g: The most honored seat.

chapters.n: The host might then ask you to give up your seat, and you’d have to move — embarrassed — to the lowest place, the only one left.

f.g: Make room for this man.

chapters.n: Instead, take the lowest seat. If the host moves you up, you’ll be honored in front of everyone. This echoes Proverbs.

f.g: Honor, respect (the older English meaning).

chapters.n: The principle reaches beyond dinner parties: those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and the humble will be exalted.

f.w: whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased

f.g: Brought low.

chapters.n: Jesus then speaks to the host: don’t invite only friends, family, and rich neighbors who will repay you with invitations of their own.

f.g: Repayment.

chapters.n: Instead, invite those who can never repay — the poor, the disabled, the blind. Such people were often excluded from social life.

f.g: Crippled or disabled.

chapters.n: You will be blessed precisely because they can’t pay you back. God Himself will reward you at the resurrection of the righteous.
A guest piously remarks how blessed it will be to feast in God’s kingdom. Jesus uses this comment to ask whether they will actually accept the invitation.

f.w: eat bread in the kingdom of God
f.g: The Messianic banquet — a common Jewish image of the coming kingdom.

chapters.n: A man prepares a great banquet and sends out many invitations.

f.w: A certain man made a great supper

chapters.n: Custom was to send a first invitation, then a servant to announce when the meal was ready. Now the time has come: everything is ready.
Yet everyone makes excuses. The first says he must go see a field he bought — though no one buys land without inspecting it first.

f.g: All alike, as if by agreement.
I must go.

chapters.n: Another says he has bought five pairs of oxen and needs to test them — another flimsy excuse for something that could wait.

f.g: Ten oxen — a sign of wealth.
Test.

chapters.n: A third says he just got married and can’t come. Good things — property, work, family — can crowd out God’s invitation.
The angry host sends his servant quickly into the town’s streets to bring in the poor, disabled, and blind — the very people Jesus just said to invite.

f.g: Lame.

chapters.n: The servant reports it is done, but there is still room. God’s house has space for more.

f.g: Heaven has room for all who will come.

chapters.n: The master sends him beyond the town to the roads and hedges — a picture of the gospel going to the Gentiles. “Compel” here means to urge strongly, not to force.

f.g: Country roads and fences, where travelers and outcasts might be.
Urge them earnestly, overcoming their sense that they are unworthy.

chapters.n: Those who refused the invitation will not taste the feast. The door was open; they chose not to enter.

f.w: none of those men which were bidden

chapters.n: Huge crowds are following Jesus. He turns to tell them what following Him really requires.

f.g: Many were enthusiastic but hadn’t yet counted the cost.

chapters.n: “Hate” is a Hebrew way of saying “love less.” Devotion to Christ must come first, above even family and one’s own life. Matthew says “loveth more than me.”

f.g: A Semitic idiom of comparison: to love less, to put second.

chapters.n: A disciple must carry his own cross and follow — willing to suffer and even die for Christ.
Before building a tower, a wise person calculates whether he has enough resources to finish it.

f.g: Estimates the expense.

chapters.n: Otherwise, he might lay the foundation and run out of money, becoming a laughingstock.

f.g: Lest perhaps.

chapters.n: Onlookers will mock: he started but couldn’t finish. A half-hearted disciple is like an abandoned building project.
A king facing an army twice his size would carefully consider whether he could win before going to battle.

f.g: Deliberates, takes counsel.

chapters.n: If not, he would send messengers early to negotiate peace. Discipleship requires that same clear-eyed reckoning.

f.g: A delegation of ambassadors.

chapters.n: The bottom line: anyone unwilling to give up everything cannot be Christ’s disciple. This means willingness to put all on the altar.

f.w: forsaketh not all that he hath

chapters.n: Salt is valuable, but salt that has lost its flavor is useless. Disciples who lose their distinctiveness lose their purpose.

f.g: Flavor.

chapters.n: Tasteless salt isn’t even useful as fertilizer — it’s just thrown out. Jesus closes with His call to truly listen.

f.g: Manure pile, used to fertilize fields.

f.w: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear

chapters.n: Tax collectors and notorious sinners crowd around to hear Jesus. People whom respectable society shunned feel welcome with Him.

f.g: Jewish tax collectors working for Rome, widely viewed as traitors and cheats.

chapters.n: The religious leaders grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and even eats with them — sharing a meal meant friendship and acceptance. The three parables that follow answer this complaint.

f.g: Grumbled, complained under their breath.

chapters.n: Jesus responds with a parable — really a set of three stories about something lost and found.

f.g: Luke 15 contains three linked parables: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son.

chapters.n: A shepherd who loses one sheep out of a hundred leaves the ninety-nine and searches until he finds it. Every single one matters to him.

f.g: The shepherd doesn’t give up.

chapters.n: When he finds it, there is no scolding — he joyfully lifts it onto his shoulders and carries it home. This is how the Good Shepherd treats the lost.
He gathers friends and neighbors to celebrate with him. Finding the lost is a joy meant to be shared.

f.g: Notice the shepherd’s joy is the center of the story.

chapters.n: Heaven rejoices more over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine who think they need no repentance — a pointed word to the self-righteous critics.

f.w: joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth

f.g: Righteous people — or those who consider themselves so.

chapters.n: A woman loses one of ten silver coins. She lights a lamp in her dim house, sweeps every corner, and searches carefully until she finds it.

f.g: Greek drachma, about a day’s wage. Some think the ten coins may have been part of a dowry or headdress.
Village homes had few windows and needed a lamp even by day.

chapters.n: She too calls her friends to celebrate. The lost coin couldn’t find its way back — someone had to search for it.

f.w: the piece which I had lost
f.g: The coin didn’t wander off; it was lost through neglect or accident.

chapters.n: In the same way, the angels of God rejoice whenever a sinner repents.

f.w: joy in the presence of the angels of God

chapters.n: The third story, often called the Prodigal Son, is really about a father and two sons — each lost in a different way.

f.g: The younger represents open sinners; the elder resembles the grumbling Pharisees.

chapters.n: The younger son demands his inheritance now — essentially treating his father as already dead. The father, with painful patience, agrees.

f.w: the portion of goods that falleth to me
f.g: His share of the estate; a younger son normally received one-third.
His property, livelihood.

chapters.n: He quickly converts everything to cash, heads to a faraway land, and squanders it all on reckless, wild living.

f.g: Scattered his wealth.
Wasteful, reckless, dissolute.

chapters.n: Just as his money runs out, a severe famine hits. Now he is in desperate need.

f.g: In need, lacking necessities.

chapters.n: He hires himself out to a foreigner who sends him to feed pigs — the lowest humiliation imaginable for a Jew, since swine were unclean.

f.g: Attached himself — almost begged for work.

chapters.n: He is so hungry he envies the pigs their feed of pods, and no one gives him anything.

f.g: Would gladly have.
Carob pods — cheap animal feed eaten by people only in extreme poverty.

chapters.n: Then he “came to himself” — he woke up to reality. Even his father’s hired workers have plenty while he is starving.

f.g: A turning point: repentance begins with seeing clearly.

chapters.n: He resolves to go home and confess that he has sinned against God and against his father.

f.w: I will arise and go to my father

f.g: A reverent Jewish way of saying “against God.”

chapters.n: He plans to ask to be treated as a hired worker. He no longer feels worthy to be called a son.

f.g: Day laborers, below even household servants in security.

chapters.n: The father has been watching. Seeing him far off, he is filled with compassion and runs — undignified for an older man — to embrace and kiss his son before a word is spoken. This is Heavenly Father’s love.

f.g: Threw his arms around him.

f.w: when he was yet a great way off

chapters.n: The son begins his confession, but the father doesn’t even let him finish the part about becoming a hired servant.

f.g: Before you, against you.

chapters.n: The father restores him fully: the best robe (honor), a ring (authority and family standing), and sandals (servants went barefoot; sons wore shoes).

f.g: A signet ring signified sonship and authority.

chapters.n: He orders the fattened calf — saved for the biggest celebrations — to be prepared for a feast.

f.g: A calf specially fed for a special occasion.

chapters.n: The father explains: my son was dead and is alive; he was lost and is found. Repentance is like coming back to life.

f.w: was dead, and is alive again

chapters.n: The elder son, coming in from working the fields, hears music and dancing from the house.

f.g: Music.

chapters.n: He asks a servant what is going on rather than going straight in.

f.g: What was happening.

chapters.n: The servant explains that his brother is home safe and the father has thrown a feast.

f.g: In good health.

chapters.n: The elder brother refuses to go in. Once again the father goes out — this time to plead with his other son. He seeks both of his lost children.

f.g: Pleaded with him, urged him.

chapters.n: The elder son complains about years of slaving and obedience without even a goat for a party. He sees himself as a servant, not a son, and resents grace shown to another.

f.g: A young goat — far less than a fatted calf.

f.w: these many years do I serve thee
f.g: Literally “slave for you” — he has missed the joy of sonship.

chapters.n: He won’t even say “my brother” — only “this son of yours.” He highlights his brother’s sins and resents the celebration.

f.g: Prostitutes.
Note he distances himself from his brother.

chapters.n: The father answers tenderly: “Son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours.” The elder son’s inheritance was never in danger.

f.w: all that I have is thine

chapters.n: We had to celebrate — your brother was dead and is alive again, lost and now found. The story ends without telling us if the elder son went in, inviting each listener to decide how they will respond.

f.g: Right, fitting.
The father gently reminds him: he is still your brother.

chapters.n: Jesus tells His disciples about a wealthy man whose estate manager was reported for mismanaging and wasting his property.

f.g: A household manager who handled the owner’s business and accounts.
The same word used of the prodigal son “wasting” his substance.

chapters.n: The owner calls him in, demands a final accounting, and tells him he is fired.

f.w: give an account of thy stewardship

chapters.n: The steward panics. He’s not strong enough for manual labor and too proud to beg. What will he do?

f.g: Digging was hard manual labor for the lowest workers.

chapters.n: He comes up with a plan to make friends who will take him in once he loses his job.

f.g: I know what I’ll do.

chapters.n: Before word of his firing gets out, he calls in each of his master’s debtors one by one.

f.g: Probably tenant farmers or merchants who owed goods.

chapters.n: One owes a hundred measures of olive oil; the steward has him rewrite the bill for fifty — a huge discount.

f.g: About 800–900 gallons — the yield of roughly 150 olive trees.
The written promissory note.

chapters.n: Another owes a hundred measures of wheat; the steward reduces it to eighty. Now these men owe him a favor.

f.g: Eighty (four times twenty).
A large quantity — perhaps the harvest of about a hundred acres.

chapters.n: The master grudgingly admires his shrewdness — not his dishonesty. Jesus observes that worldly people are often more clever about their futures than God’s people are about eternity.

f.g: Praised — for his foresight, not his ethics.

chapters.n: Use worldly wealth to bless others and build eternal friendships, so that when money fails, you will be welcomed into eternal homes. Money is a tool for heavenly purposes.

f.g: An Aramaic word for wealth or possessions, here almost personified as a rival god.

chapters.n: How we handle small things shows how we’ll handle big ones. Faithfulness and dishonesty both begin in little matters.

f.w: faithful in that which is least

chapters.n: If we can’t be trusted with money, which is temporary, how can God trust us with true, eternal riches?
Everything we have really belongs to God; we are stewards. Faithfulness with what is His prepares us to receive what will eternally be our own.
You can’t be fully devoted to two masters. Ultimately, you must choose: God or money.

f.w: No servant can serve two masters

chapters.n: The Pharisees, who loved money, hear this and sneer at Jesus.

f.g: Lovers of money.
Scoffed, literally “turned up their noses.”

chapters.n: Jesus replies that they make themselves look righteous to people, but God sees their hearts. What society prizes, God often despises. The JST adds several verses here expanding His reply.

f.g: Something detestable.

chapters.n: The law and prophets pointed forward until John the Baptist. Now God’s kingdom is being preached, and people are pushing eagerly to get in.

f.g: Forces their way in — eagerly entering.

chapters.n: This doesn’t mean God’s law is discarded. Heaven and earth would vanish sooner than the smallest part of it would fail; Christ came to fulfill it.

f.g: A tiny stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another.

f.w: one tittle of the law to fail

chapters.n: As an example of the law’s enduring force, Jesus upholds the sacredness of marriage. Divorcing to marry someone else is adultery — a stricter standard than the Pharisees taught.

f.g: Divorces her.

chapters.n: Another story: a rich man dresses in royal purple and expensive linen and feasts luxuriously every day.

f.g: Purple dye was very costly; this was the clothing of royalty and the extremely rich.
Lavishly.

chapters.n: At his gate lies a beggar named Lazarus, covered in sores. He is the only character in Jesus’ parables given a name — the poor man is known to God.

f.g: A form of Eleazar, “God has helped.”
Placed there by others — he couldn’t walk.

chapters.n: He longs for scraps from the rich man’s table. Only street dogs pay him attention, licking his sores.

f.g: Scraps; sometimes bread used to wipe hands was thrown under the table.

chapters.n: Both die. Angels carry Lazarus to Abraham’s side — a place of honor and rest. The rich man is simply buried.

f.g: A Jewish image of paradise — reclining next to Abraham at the heavenly feast.

chapters.n: In the spirit world the rich man is in torment. He can see Abraham far away with Lazarus beside him.

f.g: Greek hadēs — the spirit world; latter-day scripture calls this part of it spirit prison.

chapters.n: Now he begs for mercy — but still treats Lazarus as a servant to be sent on an errand.

f.g: Scripture often describes the anguish of a guilty conscience as fire.

chapters.n: Abraham gently reminds him: you had your comforts in life; Lazarus had suffering. Now their situations are reversed.

f.g: Abraham still addresses him kindly.

f.w: thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things

chapters.n: A great gulf separates the two places, and no one can cross. Latter-day revelation teaches that Christ, after His death, bridged this gulf by organizing the preaching of the gospel to the spirits in prison.
The rich man then asks Abraham to send Lazarus to his family’s home.

f.g: His family.

chapters.n: He has five brothers and wants Lazarus to warn them so they won’t end up in this place of torment.

f.g: Warn them solemnly.

chapters.n: Abraham answers that they already have the scriptures — Moses and the prophets. Let them listen to those.

f.g: The Hebrew scriptures, our Old Testament.

chapters.n: The rich man insists that a visitor from the dead would surely convince them to repent.
Abraham’s answer is sobering: if they ignore the scriptures, not even a resurrection will persuade them. Soon, Jesus Himself would rise from the dead — and many would still not believe.

f.w: though one rose from the dead

chapters.n: In a fallen world, things that cause people to stumble will happen. But Jesus warns that those who lead others into sin carry a heavy responsibility.

f.g: Greek skandala — stumbling blocks, traps that cause someone to fall into sin.

chapters.n: It would be better to be drowned with a heavy stone tied around one’s neck than to cause a vulnerable or new believer to fall away.

f.g: A large stone used for grinding grain.
Children, and also humble or new disciples.

chapters.n: Watch yourselves. If someone wrongs you, address it honestly; if they repent, forgive them. Correction and forgiveness work together.

f.g: Sin against, wrong.

chapters.n: Even if it happens seven times in one day, keep forgiving. There is no limit on forgiveness for the repentant.
Hearing how high the standard is, the apostles plead: give us more faith!

Jesus replies that even tiny faith — like a mustard seed — can do the impossible, like commanding a deep-rooted tree to replant itself in the sea. The issue is not the size of faith but its genuineness.

f.g: A black mulberry tree, known for its deep, extensive roots.

f.w: faith as a grain of mustard seed

chapters.n: Jesus describes a servant coming in from plowing or shepherding. Would his master tell him to sit down and eat first?

f.g: Immediately (the older English meaning).

chapters.n: No — the master would expect him to prepare dinner and serve first, then eat afterward.

f.g: Eat supper.
Tuck in your robe and get ready to serve.

chapters.n: The master doesn’t thank the servant for simply doing what was expected.

f.g: I think not.

chapters.n: Likewise, when we obey God, we haven’t earned special credit — we’ve done our duty. Service done in humility, not pride, pleases God. King Benjamin taught the same.
Still traveling toward Jerusalem, Jesus passes along the border region between Samaria and Galilee.

f.w: the midst of Samaria and Galilee
f.g: Probably along the boundary between the two regions.

chapters.n: Ten men with leprosy meet Him at a village, keeping their distance as the law required of those with skin diseases.

f.g: People with a contagious skin disease (not always modern leprosy) who were isolated from society.

chapters.n: They shout together for mercy. Shared suffering has erased the line between Jew and Samaritan.

f.g: Greek epistatēs, “chief” or “commander.”

chapters.n: Jesus tells them to go show themselves to the priests — the procedure for someone already healed. As they obey in faith, they are cleansed on the way.
One of them, realizing he is healed, turns back, loudly praising God.

f.g: The same word used for repentance — turning around.

chapters.n: He falls at Jesus’ feet in gratitude. Luke saves a twist for the end: this grateful man is a Samaritan, an outsider.
Jesus asks: weren’t ten healed? Where are the other nine?
Only this foreigner came back to give glory to God. Gratitude is rarer than blessings.

f.g: Foreigner — one not of Israel.

chapters.n: Jesus tells him to rise and go: his faith has made him whole. All ten were cleansed in body, but this one received something more — wholeness and salvation.

f.g: Greek sōzō — saved, healed, made complete.

chapters.n: The Pharisees ask when God’s kingdom will arrive. Jesus says it won’t come with dramatic signs to be watched for and charted.

f.g: With visible signs that can be watched for and calculated.

chapters.n: No one will need to point “here” or “there,” because the kingdom is already among them — present in Jesus Himself.

f.g: Greek can mean “in your midst.” JST Luke 17:21: “the kingdom of God has already come unto you.”

chapters.n: Jesus warns His disciples of coming days when they will long for even one day of His presence and will not have it.

f.w: the days of the Son of man
f.g: The time of Jesus’ presence — now in mortality and later at His coming.

chapters.n: People will claim the Messiah is here or there. Don’t chase after them. False Christs will come.
His Second Coming won’t be a secret: it will be as unmistakable as lightning flashing across the whole sky.
But before glory comes suffering. He must first suffer greatly and be rejected by His own generation.

f.w: first must he suffer many things

chapters.n: The world at His coming will be like the world in Noah’s day.

f.g: Greek form of the name Noah.

f.w: as it was in the days of Noe

chapters.n: People carried on with normal life — eating, drinking, marrying — paying no attention to warnings until the flood swept them away.

f.w: until the day that Noe entered into the ark

chapters.n: Lot’s day was the same: buying, selling, farming, and building, unaware of what was coming.

f.g: Built.

chapters.n: The very day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulfur rained down and destroyed the city.

f.g: Sulfur, which burns with intense heat.

chapters.n: It will be just like that when the Son of Man is revealed — sudden, while people are absorbed in ordinary life.

f.g: Unveiled, made fully visible.

f.w: the day when the Son of man is revealed

chapters.n: On that day, don’t go back for possessions. Someone on the roof shouldn’t go down for belongings; someone in a field shouldn’t turn back.

f.g: Belongings.

chapters.n: Just three words: Remember Lot’s wife. She looked back with longing at what she left and was lost.
Clinging to this life means losing it; giving it up for God means keeping it.

f.g: Literally “keep it alive.”

chapters.n: On that night, two people may share a bed; one will be taken and one left. Judgment will divide even the closest companions.
Two women grinding grain together — one taken, the other left. Life will be going on as usual.

f.g: Women commonly ground grain together at a hand mill each morning.

chapters.n: Two men working in a field — one taken, one left. Readiness is personal; no one can be prepared for another.

f.w: Two men shall be in the field
f.g: This verse is absent from many early Greek manuscripts but appears in Matthew 24:40.

chapters.n: The disciples ask where this will happen. Jesus answers with a proverb: where the carcass is, the vultures gather. The JST explains that the “body” is where the Saints are gathered.

f.g: Greek aetos can mean eagles or vultures.

chapters.n: Luke tells us the point before the story: keep praying and don’t lose heart, even when answers seem slow.

f.g: Lose heart, give up.

chapters.n: A judge in some town had no reverence for God and no concern for people — the worst kind of person to hold power.

f.g: Respected, cared about.

chapters.n: A widow — among the most vulnerable people in that society — keeps coming to him, demanding justice against someone who has wronged her.

f.g: Widows often had no legal advocate; the law commanded special care for them.
Give me justice; vindicate me.

chapters.n: For a while he refuses. But eventually he admits to himself that, though he cares nothing for God or anyone...

f.g: In private reasoning — Luke often lets us hear characters’ thoughts.

chapters.n: ...this widow is wearing him out. He’ll give her justice just to get rid of her before she exhausts him.

f.g: Literally “give me a black eye” — wear me down.

chapters.n: Jesus says: listen to what even this unjust judge concluded.

f.g: The judge is a contrast to God, not a picture of Him.

chapters.n: If an unjust judge eventually helps, won’t a righteous and loving God help His own people who cry out to Him day and night? His timing may seem long, but He cares.

f.g: God’s chosen, covenant people.

f.w: though he bear long with them

chapters.n: God will bring justice, and when it comes it will be swift. The real question is whether Christ will find people still faithfully praying when He returns.

f.w: shall he find faith on the earth?

chapters.n: The next parable is aimed at people who were sure of their own goodness and looked down on everyone else.

f.g: Looked down on with contempt.

chapters.n: Two men go up to the temple to pray: a Pharisee, admired for strict observance, and a tax collector, despised as a collaborator and cheat.

f.g: A tax collector for Rome.
The temple sat on a hill, so worshippers always “went up.”

chapters.n: The Pharisee stands and prays “with himself” — really to himself. He thanks God that he isn’t like other people, including that tax collector over there.

f.g: Swindlers, people who rob by force or fraud.
Possibly “prayed to himself” — his prayer is self-focused.

chapters.n: He lists his religious achievements, going beyond what the law required. His prayer asks for nothing because he thinks he needs nothing.

f.w: I fast twice in the week
f.g: The law required fasting only on the Day of Atonement; devout Pharisees fasted Mondays and Thursdays.

chapters.n: The tax collector stands at a distance, won’t even look up, and beats his chest in sorrow. His prayer is just: God, be merciful to me, a sinner.

f.g: Beat his chest — a gesture of deep grief and remorse.

f.w: God be merciful to me a sinner
f.g: The Greek suggests “make atonement for me.”

chapters.n: Jesus declares that the tax collector, not the Pharisee, went home justified — right with God. The humble are lifted up; the proud are brought down.

f.g: Declared righteous, put right with God.

f.w: he that humbleth himself shall be exalted

chapters.n: Parents bring even babies for Jesus to bless, but the disciples try to stop them, thinking He is too busy for children.

f.g: Greek brephē — babies.

chapters.n: Jesus calls the children to Him. God’s kingdom belongs to those who are like them — humble, trusting, and teachable.

f.w: Suffer little children to come unto me

f.g: Allow, let.

chapters.n: Anyone who doesn’t receive the kingdom with a child’s trust and humility will not enter it.
A ruler asks the great question: what must I do to inherit eternal life? He seems sincere but thinks of it as something to earn.

f.g: A leader — Matthew says he was young; all three Gospels say he was rich.

chapters.n: Jesus asks why he calls Him good, since only God is good. He is inviting the man to think about who Jesus really is.
Jesus lists commandments about how we treat others, from the Ten Commandments.
The ruler says he has kept them all since he was young. He may well have, outwardly.

f.g: Since boyhood.

chapters.n: Jesus sees what holds him back: he still lacks one thing. Sell everything, give to the poor, and follow Me. The invitation is to discipleship, not just a donation.
He becomes deeply sad, because he is extremely rich. His wealth had a stronger hold on him than he realized.

f.g: Grieved, distressed.

chapters.n: Seeing his sorrow, Jesus remarks how hard it is for the wealthy to enter God’s kingdom.

f.g: With what difficulty.

chapters.n: It’s easier for a camel — the largest animal in the region — to pass through a needle’s eye. The image is deliberately impossible.

f.w: a camel to go through a needle's eye
f.g: A vivid exaggeration typical of Jewish teaching; the popular “narrow gate” explanation is a later idea.

chapters.n: The hearers are stunned. Many saw wealth as a sign of God’s favor. If the rich can’t be saved, who can?

f.g: Their surprise reveals their assumption that riches meant blessing.

chapters.n: What is impossible for humans is possible for God. Salvation is always His gift, for rich and poor alike.
Peter points out that the disciples have left everything to follow Him.
Jesus assures them that anyone who has given up home or family for God’s kingdom...

f.w: for the kingdom of God's sake
f.g: For the sake of God’s work, not for selfish reasons.

chapters.n: ...will receive much more in this life and eternal life in the world to come. No sacrifice for God goes unrewarded.

f.g: Many times as much.

chapters.n: Taking the Twelve aside, Jesus tells them again that in Jerusalem everything the prophets wrote about the Son of Man will be fulfilled.

f.w: all things that are written by the prophets

chapters.n: He will be handed over to the Romans, mocked, insulted, and spit upon. This is His most detailed prediction of His suffering.

f.g: Treated with insolence and abuse.

chapters.n: They will flog Him and kill Him, but on the third day He will rise again. The Resurrection is always part of His prediction.

f.g: Flog with a whip — a brutal Roman punishment.

f.w: the third day he shall rise again

chapters.n: The Twelve don’t understand any of it. The meaning is hidden from them until after the Resurrection.

f.w: this saying was hid from them

chapters.n: Near Jericho, a blind man sits by the road begging. Mark names him Bartimaeus.

f.g: An ancient oasis city near the Jordan, about 17 miles northeast of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Hearing a crowd passing, he asks what’s happening.

f.g: What was going on.

chapters.n: They tell him Jesus of Nazareth is passing by — perhaps his only chance.

f.g: A common way to identify Him by His hometown.

chapters.n: He cries out, calling Jesus “Son of David” — a messianic title. Though blind, he sees who Jesus really is.

f.g: A title for the promised Messiah, descended from King David.

chapters.n: People at the front scold him to be quiet, but he shouts all the louder. His persistence is the kind of prayer Jesus praised at the start of this chapter.

f.g: Be quiet.

chapters.n: Jesus stops — the whole procession halts for a single beggar — and has him brought over.

f.g: He stopped walking.

chapters.n: Jesus asks what he wants. The answer seems obvious, but Jesus invites him to express his faith and desire.

f.w: What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee?

chapters.n: Jesus says: receive your sight; your faith has saved you.

f.g: Greek sōzō — healed and saved.

chapters.n: He sees immediately and follows Jesus, praising God. The crowd joins in praise. Once blind, he now walks the road to Jerusalem as a disciple.

f.g: He became a disciple, joining the journey to Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Jesus enters Jericho, the last major stop on His journey before the climb to Jerusalem.

f.g: A prosperous city on a major trade route — a natural place for a tax office.

chapters.n: Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector — a supervisor over other tax collectors — and he is wealthy, likely from overcharging people. Ironically, his name means “pure” or “innocent.”

f.g: From the Hebrew Zakkai, “pure, righteous.”
A head tax collector, the only time this title appears in the New Testament.

chapters.n: He wants to see who Jesus is, but he is short and can’t see over the crowd — a crowd that may not have been eager to make room for him.

f.g: Crowd.
Short.

chapters.n: Forgetting his dignity, he runs ahead and climbs a tree along the route. Wealthy men didn’t usually run or climb trees — his desire outweighs his pride.

f.g: A sycamore-fig, with low, spreading branches easy to climb — not the same as an American sycamore.

chapters.n: Jesus stops, looks up, and calls him by name, inviting Himself to stay at his house today. Zacchaeus was seeking Jesus, but Jesus was seeking him.

f.g: Jesus knows his name before they are introduced.
Stay.

chapters.n: Zacchaeus hurries down and welcomes Jesus with joy. Being known and wanted by Jesus changes him.
The crowd grumbles that Jesus is going to be the guest of a notorious sinner. To eat with someone was to accept him.

f.g: Grumbled.

chapters.n: Zacchaeus stands and makes a public commitment: half his wealth to the poor, and fourfold repayment to anyone he cheated — far more than the law required. This is repentance in action.

f.g: The law of Moses required fourfold restitution only for certain thefts; usually it was the amount plus one-fifth.
Extortion — demanding more than was owed.

chapters.n: Jesus declares that salvation has come to this household. Despised as he was, Zacchaeus is a true son of Abraham, an heir of the covenant.
This verse sums up Jesus’ entire mission: He came to seek out and save the lost.

f.w: to seek and to save that which was lost

chapters.n: Near Jerusalem, many expect God’s kingdom to appear immediately in political triumph. Jesus tells a parable to correct that expectation: there will be a delay.

f.g: They expected Jesus to establish His kingdom on arrival in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: A nobleman travels to a distant land to be appointed king, then plans to return. Jesus would go to heaven and return later in glory. Listeners might also recall Archelaus, a son of Herod who went to Rome seeking kingship.

f.g: Historically, Herod’s sons went to Rome to have their rule confirmed by Caesar.

chapters.n: Before leaving, he gives each of ten servants one pound and tells them to do business with it until he returns. Each receives the same trust.

f.g: Greek mna (mina), about 100 days’ wages.
Do business, put it to work.

chapters.n: But his citizens hate him and send word that they don’t want him as king. Some reject Christ’s rule outright.

f.w: We will not have this man to reign over us

chapters.n: Having been crowned, he returns and calls in his servants to see what each gained. Christ will return and ask for an accounting.
The first servant has multiplied the money tenfold.

f.g: He humbly credits the master’s money, not himself.

chapters.n: The master praises him: faithful in a very small thing, he now receives authority over ten cities. Faithfulness is rewarded far out of proportion.
The second servant has made five pounds.

f.g: A good result, though less than the first.

chapters.n: He receives five cities. Reward matches faithfulness.

f.g: Responsibility grows according to diligence.

chapters.n: Another servant returns the original pound, which he has kept wrapped in a cloth. He did nothing with it.

f.g: A cloth, such as a sweat cloth or handkerchief.

chapters.n: He blames his master, calling him harsh and demanding. Fear and a false view of the master paralyzed him.

f.g: Strict, harsh, severe.

chapters.n: The master judges him by his own words: if you believed I was so demanding, you should have acted accordingly.

f.w: Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee

chapters.n: He could at least have deposited the money with bankers to earn interest. Doing nothing was the real failure.

f.g: Interest (not necessarily excessive, as the modern word implies).

chapters.n: The master orders the pound taken from him and given to the servant who has ten.
Bystanders object: but he already has ten! It seems unfair.

f.g: A parenthetical protest from the listeners.

chapters.n: Those who use what they have receive more; those who neglect their gifts lose them. Spiritual gifts grow through use.

f.w: unto every one which hath shall be given

chapters.n: The enemies who rejected the king’s rule face judgment. The parable ends with a sober warning that rejecting Christ has consequences.

f.g: Ancient kings dealt harshly with rebels; the image depicts final judgment.

chapters.n: Having finished speaking, Jesus leads the way up the steep road to Jerusalem — determined, walking ahead of His disciples.

f.g: From Jericho the road climbs about 3,500 feet in roughly 17 miles.

chapters.n: Approaching villages on the Mount of Olives just east of Jerusalem, He sends two disciples ahead.

f.g: Villages on the eastern slopes of the Mount of Olives; Bethany was home to Mary, Martha, and Lazarus.

chapters.n: They will find a colt that no one has ever ridden. An animal never used for ordinary work was considered fit for sacred purposes.

f.g: A young donkey (Matthew and John specify a donkey).

chapters.n: If anyone asks, they are to say that the Lord needs it. Jesus knows what they will encounter.

f.w: the Lord hath need of him
f.g: “Lord” here may mean Jesus, or the owner may have been a disciple who would understand.

chapters.n: They go and find everything exactly as He said.

f.w: found even as he had said

chapters.n: As they untie the colt, its owners ask what they are doing.

f.g: Untying.

chapters.n: They give the answer Jesus told them, and the owners allow it.

f.w: The Lord hath need of him
f.g: Obedience to precise instructions brings the expected result.

chapters.n: They throw their cloaks on the colt as a saddle and help Jesus mount. Riding a donkey fulfilled Zechariah’s prophecy of a humble, peaceful king.
People spread their cloaks on the road before Him, a royal welcome like that given to Israel’s ancient kings.

f.w: spread their clothes in the way

chapters.n: As the road descends the Mount of Olives with Jerusalem in full view, His disciples burst into loud praise for all the miracles they have seen.

f.w: the descent of the mount of Olives
f.g: From here the whole city and temple would come suddenly into view.

chapters.n: They hail Him as King, quoting Psalm 118. Their “peace in heaven” echoes the angels’ song at His birth.

f.w: Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord

chapters.n: Some Pharisees, alarmed at the royal claims, tell Jesus to silence His followers.

f.g: Messianic claims could provoke Roman retaliation.

chapters.n: Jesus answers that if they were silent, the very stones would cry out. Creation itself must acknowledge its King.

f.w: the stones would immediately cry out

chapters.n: Coming near, Jesus sees the city and weeps over it — sobbing aloud. Amid the cheering, He grieves for those who will reject Him.

f.g: A word meaning to weep aloud, to lament.

chapters.n: If only Jerusalem had recognized, on this day of all days, what would bring it peace! But now it is hidden from them. There is a play on words: Jerusalem means “foundation of peace.”

f.w: the things which belong unto thy peace

chapters.n: He foresees enemy armies building siege works around the city and surrounding it on all sides. The Romans did exactly this in AD 70.

f.g: Build a siege rampart or palisade.
Surround you.

chapters.n: They will flatten the city and its people, leaving not one stone on another — because Jerusalem did not recognize the time when God came to visit and save it.

f.g: The time when God came in person to bless and redeem them.

f.w: not leave in thee one stone upon another

chapters.n: Jesus enters the temple and begins driving out the merchants. Selling animals and exchanging money had turned the Court of the Gentiles into a marketplace.

f.g: Merchants selling sacrificial animals, often at inflated prices.

chapters.n: He quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah: God’s house should be a house of prayer, but they have turned it into a hideout for robbers.

f.w: My house is the house of prayer

chapters.n: He teaches in the temple every day. Meanwhile the chief priests, scribes, and leading men look for a way to kill Him.

f.g: Leading citizens, probably elders of the Sanhedrin council.

chapters.n: They can’t find a way, because the people hang on His every word. His popularity protects Him — for now.

f.g: Literally “hung upon him, listening.”

chapters.n: During the last week of His life, while Jesus teaches in the temple, a delegation of chief priests, scribes, and elders — representatives of the ruling council — confronts Him.

f.w: the chief priests and the scribes came upon him with the elders
f.g: These three groups made up the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council.

chapters.n: They demand to know His authority. Who gave Him the right to clear the temple and teach there? They control the temple and never authorized Him.
Jesus answers with a question of His own, a common rabbinic way of debating.

f.w: I will also ask you one thing
f.g: Answering a question with a question was a respected teaching method.

chapters.n: Was John’s baptism authorized by God or merely human? The answer to this question also answers theirs, since John testified of Jesus.

f.g: John’s whole ministry, of which baptism was the sign.

chapters.n: They huddle privately and see the trap: if they say “from heaven,” He’ll ask why they didn’t believe John.

f.g: Debated among themselves.

chapters.n: If they say “from men,” the crowd might stone them, since the people firmly believe John was a prophet. They are more concerned with public opinion than with truth.

f.w: they be persuaded that John was a prophet

chapters.n: So they claim not to know. Their non-answer exposes that they aren’t really seeking truth.

f.g: From where.
