chapters.n: Since they refuse to answer honestly, Jesus declines to answer them. Those unwilling to accept truth don’t receive more of it.
Jesus tells the people a parable. A man plants a vineyard, rents it to tenant farmers, and leaves for a long time. Isaiah had used the vineyard as a symbol of Israel.

f.g: Tenant farmers, vinedressers.

chapters.n: At harvest the owner sends a servant to collect his share. The tenants beat him and send him away with nothing.

f.g: At harvest time, when rent was due in produce.

chapters.n: He sends a second servant, who is beaten and humiliated.

f.g: Treated him disgracefully.

chapters.n: A third is wounded and thrown out. These servants represent the prophets God sent to Israel, many of whom were mistreated.
The owner decides to send his beloved son, hoping they will respect him. The phrase “beloved son” echoes the Father’s words at Jesus’ baptism and Transfiguration.

f.g: Respect him.

chapters.n: The tenants recognize the heir and plot to kill him, imagining they will keep the vineyard. Jesus is openly describing the leaders’ plot against Him.
They throw him out of the vineyard and kill him. Jesus would be crucified outside Jerusalem’s walls. He then asks what the owner will do.

f.w: cast him out of the vineyard

chapters.n: The owner will destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others. The listeners recoil in horror: may it never be!

f.g: Greek mē genoito — “may it never happen!”

chapters.n: Jesus looks right at them and quotes Psalm 118: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The rejected Son becomes the foundation of everything.

f.w: The stone which the builders rejected

f.g: The cornerstone or capstone — the most important stone in a building.

chapters.n: Stumbling over this stone breaks a person; having it fall on them crushes them. Rejecting Christ is ultimately self-destructive.
The leaders realize the parable is about them and want to arrest Him immediately, but they fear the crowd.

f.g: Arrest Him.

chapters.n: They send spies pretending to be sincere, hoping to catch Him in words they could use to hand Him over to the Roman governor.

f.g: Pretend to be honest inquirers.
Pontius Pilate.

chapters.n: They begin with flattery: Teacher, You are honest and impartial and teach God’s way truthfully. Their compliments are true, but they don’t mean them.

f.w: acceptest thou the person of any
f.g: Show favoritism based on someone’s status.

chapters.n: Then the trap: should we pay taxes to Caesar? Saying yes would anger Jewish patriots; saying no would be treason against Rome.

f.g: A poll tax paid directly to Rome, deeply resented by many Jews.
The Roman emperor, at this time Tiberius.

chapters.n: Jesus sees right through their scheme.

f.g: Cunning, trickery.
Test, try to trap.

chapters.n: He asks for a coin and asks whose image and inscription it bears. They answer: Caesar’s.

f.g: A denarius, a silver coin worth a day’s wage, stamped with the emperor’s portrait.
Inscription.

chapters.n: Give Caesar what bears his image, and give God what bears His image — ourselves. We have civil duties, but our whole selves belong to God.

f.w: unto God the things which be God's

chapters.n: They couldn’t trap Him publicly. Amazed at His answer, they fall silent.

f.g: Were silent.

chapters.n: Next come Sadducees, the priestly aristocratic party who denied the resurrection and accepted only the five books of Moses as authoritative.

f.g: A priestly party that rejected resurrection, angels, and spirits.

chapters.n: They cite the law of levirate marriage: if a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow and raise children in his name.

f.w: raise up seed unto his brother

chapters.n: They pose an absurd hypothetical: seven brothers. The first marries and dies childless.

f.g: An exaggerated scenario designed to ridicule belief in resurrection.

chapters.n: The second marries her and dies without children.

f.g: Married her.

chapters.n: Then the third, and so on through all seven, none leaving children.

f.g: In the same way.

chapters.n: Finally the woman dies too.

f.g: After all of them.

chapters.n: Their punchline: in the resurrection, whose wife will she be? They think the question makes resurrection look ridiculous.

f.g: They don’t believe in it; they are mocking the idea.

chapters.n: Jesus answers that people of this world marry and are given in marriage. Latter-day revelation teaches that marriages performed only by earthly authority end at death.

f.g: People of this present age.

chapters.n: Those found worthy of the resurrection don’t marry there. Latter-day Saints understand this to mean marriages are not performed after the resurrection; eternal marriage must be sealed by proper authority beforehand.

f.w: neither marry, nor are given in marriage

chapters.n: Resurrected people can never die again. They are like the angels in this respect, and are God’s children, raised to immortal life.

f.w: Neither can they die any more

f.g: Those who share in the resurrection.

chapters.n: Jesus proves the resurrection from Moses himself — the very books the Sadducees accepted. At the burning bush, God calls Himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
God isn’t the God of the dead but of the living. If He is still their God, then Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob still live to Him and will rise.
Some scribes — probably Pharisees, who believed in resurrection — compliment His answer.

f.g: Pharisees shared Jesus’ belief in resurrection and enjoyed seeing the Sadducees silenced.

chapters.n: After this, no one dares ask Him any more questions.

f.g: Dared not.

chapters.n: Now Jesus asks them a question: why do people say the Messiah is merely David’s son?

f.g: A common title for the Messiah, a descendant of David.

chapters.n: In Psalm 110, David writes that the LORD (God) said to “my Lord” (the Messiah): sit at My right hand. In Latter-day Saint understanding, this pictures the Father and the Son.

f.w: The LORD said unto my Lord

chapters.n: ...until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet — an image of total victory.

f.g: Conquerors sometimes placed their feet on defeated enemies’ necks.

chapters.n: If David calls the Messiah “Lord,” how can he be just David’s son? The Messiah must be more than a human descendant — He is David’s Lord, the Son of God.

f.w: how is he then his son?

chapters.n: With everyone listening, Jesus warns His disciples.

f.w: in the audience of all the people
f.g: In the hearing of everyone.

chapters.n: Watch out for the scribes who love flowing robes, public greetings, and the best seats at synagogues and banquets. Religious status had become their reward.

f.g: Distinguished garments marking them as scholars.
Places of honor at a meal.

chapters.n: They exploit widows — perhaps as trustees of their estates — while showing off with long prayers. Those who use religion to exploit the vulnerable will face harsher judgment.

f.g: Consume the property of widows.
For appearance.
More severe condemnation.

chapters.n: In the temple’s Court of the Women, Jesus watches wealthy people dropping their gifts into the offering chests.

f.g: Thirteen trumpet-shaped offering chests stood in the Court of the Women.

chapters.n: He also sees a poor widow put in two tiny copper coins — the smallest money there was.

f.g: Two lepta, the smallest coins in circulation — a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.

chapters.n: Jesus declares that she has given more than all the rich donors combined. God measures gifts not by amount but by sacrifice and heart.

f.w: hath cast in more than they all

chapters.n: They gave from their surplus; she gave from her poverty — everything she had to live on. Her gift came at real cost. Just before, Jesus condemned those who “devour widows’ houses.”

f.g: Extreme poverty.

f.w: all the living that she had
f.g: All she had to live on.

chapters.n: Some admire the temple’s beauty — its fine stones and donated decorations. Herod’s temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world.

f.g: Beautiful stones; some of Herod’s temple blocks were enormous, gleaming white limestone.
Votive offerings — gifts dedicated to adorn the temple.

chapters.n: Jesus warns that the day is coming when not one stone will be left standing on another. The Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70.

f.w: there shall not be left one stone upon another

chapters.n: The disciples ask when this will happen and what sign will warn them. Jesus’ answer blends the coming fall of Jerusalem with the signs of His Second Coming.
First warning: don’t be deceived. Many will come claiming to be the Christ or saying the end is near. Don’t follow them.

f.w: many shall come in my name

chapters.n: Wars and uprisings will happen, but don’t panic. These must come first, but the end won’t come immediately.

f.g: Riots, revolts, disorder.
Immediately.

chapters.n: Nations and kingdoms will fight one another.
There will be great earthquakes, famines, plagues, and terrifying signs in the heavens.

f.g: Various.
Plagues, epidemics.

chapters.n: Before all this, disciples will be arrested and persecuted, handed over to synagogues and prisons, and put on trial before kings and governors. The book of Acts records many such trials.
These trials will become opportunities to bear witness of Christ.
So decide in advance not to worry about preparing a defense.

f.g: Rehearse or prepare a speech beforehand.

chapters.n: Jesus Himself will give them words and wisdom no opponent can refute or resist. Stephen experienced exactly this.

f.w: I will give you a mouth and wisdom

f.g: Contradict.

chapters.n: Betrayal will come even from parents, siblings, relatives, and friends. Some disciples will be killed.

f.g: Relatives.

chapters.n: They will be hated everywhere because they bear Christ’s name.
Yet not a hair of their heads will perish. Even if they are killed, nothing of eternal value will be lost.

f.w: not an hair of your head perish

chapters.n: By patient endurance they will gain — or keep — their souls. Steadfastness is the path to eternal life.

f.w: In your patience possess ye your souls
f.g: By enduring, you will gain your lives.

chapters.n: When armies surround Jerusalem, they will know its destruction is near. Roman legions besieged the city in AD 70.

f.g: Surrounded by armies.
Devastation.

chapters.n: That will be the signal to flee to the mountains and not to enter the city. Early Christian tradition says believers heeded this and escaped to Pella, east of the Jordan.

f.g: The countryside.

chapters.n: These are days of judgment, when everything the prophets warned about will be fulfilled.

f.g: Days of just retribution.

chapters.n: It will be especially hard for pregnant women and nursing mothers, who cannot flee easily. Great suffering will fall on the land.

f.g: Nurse infants.

chapters.n: Many will die by the sword or be taken captive to other nations. Jerusalem will be dominated by Gentiles until the “times of the Gentiles” — the era when the gospel goes primarily to them — is complete.

f.w: the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled

f.g: Trampled, ruled over.

chapters.n: Now Jesus looks further ahead: signs in the sun, moon, and stars, nations in anguish and confusion, and the roaring of the sea and waves.

f.w: signs in the sun, and in the moon

f.g: Bewilderment, not knowing which way to turn.

chapters.n: People will faint with terror at what is coming on the world, as the very powers of heaven are shaken.

f.w: Men's hearts failing them for fear

chapters.n: Then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory — Daniel’s vision fulfilled.

f.w: the Son of man coming in a cloud

chapters.n: For the faithful these signs are not cause for terror but for hope. Stand tall and look up — your deliverance is near!

f.g: Deliverance, release.

chapters.n: Jesus gives a parable: look at the fig tree and all the trees.
When they sprout leaves, you know summer is near. You don’t need anyone to tell you.

f.g: Put out leaves.

chapters.n: Likewise, when you see these signs, you’ll know God’s kingdom is near. The righteous can read the signs of the times.

f.w: the kingdom of God is nigh at hand

chapters.n: “This generation” will see these things fulfilled. Interpreters understand this in various ways — the generation that saw Jerusalem fall, or the generation that sees the final signs begin.

f.w: This generation shall not pass away

chapters.n: Heaven and earth will pass away, but Christ’s words will never fail. His promises are more certain than the universe itself.

f.w: my words shall not pass away

chapters.n: Be careful that your hearts aren’t weighed down by overindulgence, drunkenness, and life’s worries, so that the day catches you off guard.

f.g: Weighed down, burdened.
Overindulgence; the hangover that follows a binge.

chapters.n: That day will spring like a trap on everyone on earth who is unprepared.

f.g: A trap that springs suddenly.

chapters.n: So stay alert and pray constantly, that you may have strength to come through it all and stand confidently before the Son of Man.

f.w: Watch ye therefore, and pray always
to stand before the Son of man

chapters.n: During this final week, Jesus taught in the temple each day and spent His nights on the Mount of Olives.

f.g: Stayed — perhaps camping, or lodging at Bethany on the far slope.

chapters.n: People came early each morning to hear Him in the temple. His last days were spent teaching.

f.g: They rose at dawn to hear Him.

chapters.n: The Passover is approaching — the yearly festival remembering Israel’s deliverance from Egypt, followed by a week of eating bread without yeast. Jerusalem swells with pilgrims.

f.g: A seven-day festival that began with the Passover meal.

chapters.n: The religious leaders are searching for a way to kill Jesus, but His popularity with the crowds makes them cautious.
Satan enters Judas Iscariot — one of the Twelve. Judas still chose to betray; Satan exploited a heart already open to him.

f.g: Possibly “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea — perhaps the only apostle not from Galilee.

chapters.n: Judas goes to the chief priests and the temple police officers to discuss how to hand Jesus over.

f.g: Conferred, talked.
Officers of the temple guard, a Jewish police force.

chapters.n: The leaders are delighted and agree to pay him. Matthew records the amount: thirty pieces of silver.
Judas agrees and watches for an opportunity to betray Jesus away from the crowds.

f.w: in the absence of the multitude
f.g: Privately, when no crowd could protect Him.

chapters.n: The day arrives when Passover lambs are sacrificed at the temple. Jesus, the true Lamb of God, will soon be sacrificed too.

f.g: The Passover lambs were slaughtered on the afternoon of 14 Nisan.

chapters.n: Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the Passover meal.

f.g: Preparing meant obtaining a lamb, unleavened bread, wine, and bitter herbs.

chapters.n: They ask where He wants it held. Jesus has kept the location secret, perhaps so Judas cannot betray Him before the meal.

f.g: Where do you want us to.

chapters.n: Their sign: a man carrying a water jar — unusual, since women typically carried water. Follow him to the house.

f.g: Men usually carried water in skins; a man with a jar would stand out.

chapters.n: They are to ask the homeowner, on the Teacher’s behalf, for the guest room where He will eat the Passover with His disciples.

f.g: Master or owner of the house.
Guest room.

chapters.n: He will show them a large, furnished upstairs room, ready with couches for reclining at the meal.

f.g: A room on a flat roof or second story; tradition later associated it with the gathering place in Acts.

chapters.n: Everything happens just as Jesus said, and they prepare the Passover.
When the time comes, Jesus reclines at the table with His apostles.

f.g: Literally “reclined,” the custom for the Passover meal as a sign of freedom.

chapters.n: Jesus tells them how deeply He has longed to share this Passover with them before He suffers. These are tender, intimate final hours.

f.g: A Hebrew way of expressing intense longing.

chapters.n: He will not eat it again until its meaning is fulfilled in God’s kingdom. Passover pointed to Him, and He is about to fulfill it.
He takes a cup — one of several in the Passover meal — gives thanks, and tells them to share it.

f.g: Greek eucharisteō, the root of “Eucharist.”

chapters.n: He won’t drink wine again until God’s kingdom comes. Latter-day revelation promises He will drink it again with His faithful Saints.

f.w: I will not drink of the fruit of the vine

chapters.n: Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and gives it to them: this is My body given for you; do this in remembrance of Me. He institutes the sacrament.

f.w: this do in remembrance of me

chapters.n: After the meal He takes the cup: this is the new covenant in My blood, shed for you. His death would seal a new covenant between God and His people.

f.g: The new covenant (testament and covenant translate the same Greek word).

chapters.n: Yet the betrayer is sharing this very table with Him. Sharing a meal made the betrayal even more painful.

f.w: the hand of him that betrayeth me

chapters.n: The Son of Man goes the way God has decreed, but that doesn’t excuse the betrayer. God’s foreknowledge never removes human responsibility.

f.g: A cry of grief as well as warning.

chapters.n: The apostles start asking one another who could do such a thing.

f.g: Question one another.

chapters.n: Shockingly, at this very meal, they begin arguing over who is the greatest.

f.g: A contentious dispute.

f.w: which of them should be accounted the greatest

chapters.n: Jesus contrasts His kingdom with worldly rulers, who dominate others while giving themselves flattering titles like “Benefactor.”

f.g: An honorary title rulers used for themselves (Greek Euergetēs).

chapters.n: Not so with His disciples. The greatest should be like the youngest, and the leader like a servant. Leadership in the Church is service.

f.g: The youngest in a household had the lowest status and did the menial tasks.

chapters.n: Who’s greater — the guest or the waiter? Normally the guest. But Jesus is among them as the one who serves. John records that this night He washed their feet.

f.w: I am among you as he that serveth

chapters.n: He thanks them for standing by Him through His trials.

f.g: Trials, testings.
Stayed loyal.

chapters.n: Just as the Father has given Him a kingdom, He gives them a kingdom.

f.w: I appoint unto you a kingdom
f.g: The word means to grant by covenant.

chapters.n: They will feast at His table and sit on thrones judging Israel’s twelve tribes. Latter-day revelation confirms the Twelve’s role in judging Israel.

f.w: judging the twelve tribes of Israel

chapters.n: Jesus speaks tenderly to Peter by his old name, repeating it: Satan has demanded to sift you all like wheat — shaking you violently to see what remains.

f.g: Shake in a sieve to separate grain from chaff; “you” here is plural — all the apostles.

chapters.n: But Jesus has prayed specifically for Peter that his faith won’t fail. When Peter has turned back, he must strengthen the others. Peter will lead the Church.

f.g: “Thee” here is singular — Jesus prayed for Peter personally.
When you have turned back.

chapters.n: Peter boldly insists he is ready to go to prison and even to die with Jesus.

f.w: both into prison, and to death

chapters.n: Jesus tells him that before the rooster crows that morning, Peter will deny knowing Him three times.

f.g: Roosters crow before dawn; “cockcrow” also named a watch of the night.

chapters.n: Jesus reminds them that when He sent them out with no money or supplies, they lacked nothing.

f.w: without purse, and scrip, and shoes

chapters.n: But now circumstances change: they’ll face hostility and need to provide for themselves. The talk of buying a sword is likely a vivid way of saying hard times are coming, not a call to arms.

f.g: Traveler’s bag.
Most interpreters see this as figurative; Jesus soon stops the use of a sword (v. 51).

chapters.n: Isaiah’s prophecy must be fulfilled: He will be counted among criminals. His life’s mission is reaching its end.

f.w: he was reckoned among the transgressors

chapters.n: Taking Him literally, they produce two swords. “That is enough,” He says — possibly meaning “Enough of this talk,” as they missed His point.

f.g: Perhaps “That’s enough!” — ending a conversation they had misunderstood.

chapters.n: Jesus goes out, as was His habit, to the Mount of Olives, and His disciples follow.

f.g: As He was accustomed.
Matthew and Mark name the place Gethsemane, “oil press.”

chapters.n: At the place, He urges them to pray that they won’t give in to temptation.

f.w: Pray that ye enter not into temptation

chapters.n: He moves about a stone’s throw away, kneels, and prays.

f.g: About as far as one could throw a stone.
Jews usually prayed standing; kneeling shows the intensity of this moment.

chapters.n: Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me — yet not My will, but Yours. In this submission lies the heart of the Atonement.

f.g: A biblical symbol of suffering and divine judgment.

f.w: not my will, but thine, be done

chapters.n: An angel appears from heaven to strengthen Him. Only Luke records this. Heaven sustained Him but did not remove the burden.

f.w: an angel unto him from heaven
f.g: Verses 43–44 are missing from some early manuscripts but present in many others.

chapters.n: In anguish He prays even more intensely, and His sweat falls like great drops of blood. Latter-day scripture confirms that He bled from every pore as He took upon Himself the sins and suffering of all.

f.g: Greek agōnia, intense struggle like that of an athlete or warrior.

chapters.n: Rising from prayer, He finds the disciples asleep — exhausted by grief. Luke kindly explains that sorrow had worn them out.

f.g: Only Luke gives this sympathetic reason.

chapters.n: He asks why they sleep and urges them again to get up and pray so they won’t fall into temptation.
While He is still speaking, a crowd arrives, led by Judas, who approaches to kiss Jesus — the pre-arranged signal.

f.g: A kiss was a normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher — making the betrayal all the more bitter.

chapters.n: Jesus asks: Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss? Even now, He addresses him by name, perhaps giving him a final chance.

f.w: betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?

chapters.n: Seeing what is about to happen, the disciples ask whether they should fight.

f.g: Strike.

chapters.n: One of them — John identifies him as Peter — strikes the high priest’s servant and cuts off his right ear.

f.w: the servant of the high priest
f.g: John names him Malchus.

chapters.n: Jesus says, “No more of this!” and touches the man’s ear, healing him — His last miracle of healing before the cross, performed for an enemy. Only Luke, the physician, records it.

f.g: “Let it be — no more of this.”

chapters.n: Jesus asks the leaders why they’ve come with swords and clubs as if He were a violent criminal.

f.g: Clubs.
A bandit or insurrectionist.

chapters.n: They never arrested Him in the temple during the day. But now it is their hour — the time when darkness has power.
They take Him to the high priest Caiaphas’s house. Peter follows at a distance.

f.g: The high priest was Caiaphas; his father-in-law Annas also questioned Jesus.

chapters.n: In the courtyard, people build a fire against the night chill. Peter sits down among them.

f.g: The open central courtyard of a large house.

chapters.n: A servant girl stares at him in the firelight and says he was with Jesus.

f.g: A servant girl.

chapters.n: Peter denies it: “Woman, I don’t know Him.” The first denial.
A little later someone else says he is one of them. “Man, I am not,” Peter replies. The second denial.

f.g: You are one of His disciples too.

chapters.n: About an hour later another person insists: he’s certainly one of them — he’s a Galilean. His accent gave him away.

f.g: Galileans had a distinctive regional accent.

chapters.n: Peter says he doesn’t know what they’re talking about. While the words are still in his mouth, the rooster crows. The third denial.
Only Luke records this heartbreaking moment: the Lord turns and looks at Peter. Peter remembers Jesus’ words. That look surely held sorrow — and love.

f.w: the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter
f.g: Jesus was apparently within sight across the courtyard.

chapters.n: Peter goes outside and weeps bitterly. His tears mark the beginning of his repentance; he will later become a mighty witness.
The guards holding Jesus mock Him and beat Him.

f.g: Struck Him.

chapters.n: They blindfold Him, strike His face, and taunt Him to prophesy who hit Him — mocking Him as a prophet while fulfilling His own prophecies.
They hurl many more insults at Him. Luke calls it blasphemy — they are mocking God Himself.

f.g: With irreverent insults against God.

chapters.n: At daybreak the council — elders, chief priests, and scribes — gathers and brings Him before them for a formal hearing.

f.g: The Sanhedrin, the 71-member Jewish high court.

chapters.n: They demand that He tell them plainly whether He is the Messiah. He replies that if He tells them, they won’t believe.
And if He asks them questions, they won’t answer or release Him. Their minds are made up.

f.g: The verdict was already decided.

chapters.n: From now on, He declares, the Son of Man will be seated at God’s right hand. He claims the position of divine power from Daniel and the Psalms.

f.w: sit on the right hand of the power of God

chapters.n: So they ask: are You the Son of God? He answers, “You say that I am” — a Hebrew way of saying yes, it is as you say.

f.g: An affirmative idiom: “You are right in saying I am.”

chapters.n: They need no other witnesses — they’ve heard it from His own mouth. They treat His testimony of truth as blasphemy worthy of death.

f.w: What need we any further witness?

chapters.n: The council can’t carry out an execution under Roman rule, so the whole group brings Jesus to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor.

f.g: Pontius Pilate, Roman prefect of Judea about AD 26–36, who alone could order a crucifixion.

chapters.n: They twist their religious charge into political ones Rome would care about: stirring up rebellion, opposing taxes, and claiming to be a king. The tax charge is plainly false.

f.g: Misleading the people, inciting unrest.

f.w: forbidding to give tribute to Cæsar

chapters.n: Pilate asks whether He is the King of the Jews. Jesus answers, “You say so” — affirming it, though His kingdom is not the kind Pilate fears.

f.g: An affirmative idiom: “It is as you say.”

chapters.n: Pilate declares Jesus innocent — the first of three times in this chapter that he says so.

f.w: I find no fault in this man

chapters.n: The accusers press harder, insisting He is stirring up trouble everywhere from Galilee to Judea.

f.g: Judea, or the Jewish homeland generally.
Incites.

chapters.n: Hearing the word “Galilee,” Pilate asks if Jesus is a Galilean — spotting a chance to shift responsibility.

f.g: From Galilee, which was ruled by Herod Antipas.

chapters.n: Since Galilee is Herod Antipas’s territory, Pilate sends Jesus to him. Herod is in Jerusalem for Passover. Only Luke records this hearing.

f.g: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome.

chapters.n: Herod is delighted. He has wanted to see Jesus for a long time — but only hoping to be entertained by a miracle.

f.g: For a long time.

chapters.n: Herod asks Him many questions, but Jesus says nothing at all. The man who silenced John the Baptist now receives silence from the Word of God.
The chief priests and scribes stand there making fierce accusations.

f.g: Fiercely, intensely.

chapters.n: Herod and his soldiers treat Him with contempt, mock Him, dress Him in a splendid robe as a joke king, and send Him back to Pilate.

f.g: Treated Him as worthless.
A bright, shining garment — mocking His claim to kingship.

chapters.n: That day Pilate and Herod, once enemies, become friends. Their shared contempt for Jesus unites them.

f.g: Hostile to each other.

f.w: Pilate and Herod were made friends

chapters.n: Pilate summons the chief priests, the leaders, and the people.

f.g: Members of the Jewish council.

chapters.n: He announces that he has examined Jesus publicly and found no basis for their charges.

f.w: touching those things whereof ye accuse him
f.g: Concerning your accusations.

chapters.n: Neither did Herod. Two rulers have now found Him guilty of nothing deserving death.
Pilate proposes a compromise: have Him whipped and then release Him — punishing an innocent man to appease the crowd.

f.g: Flog, scourge — a severe beating.

chapters.n: It was customary to release one prisoner at Passover. This verse is missing from some early manuscripts but matches Matthew and Mark.

f.w: of necessity he must release one

chapters.n: The crowd shouts together: Away with Him! Release Barabbas to us!

f.g: Aramaic for “son of the father” — ironically, the true Son of the Father is condemned in his place.

chapters.n: Barabbas had been imprisoned for leading a riot in the city and for murder. The crowd chooses a rebel and killer over the Prince of Peace.

f.g: Insurrection, rebellion.

chapters.n: Wanting to release Jesus, Pilate appeals to them again.

f.g: Wishing to free Him.

chapters.n: They keep shouting: Crucify Him! Crucify Him!

f.g: Crucifixion was Rome’s most shameful and agonizing execution, reserved for slaves and rebels.

chapters.n: A third time Pilate asks what evil He has done, declares he finds no grounds for death, and repeats his offer to flog and release Him.

f.g: Luke emphasizes Jesus’ innocence through Pilate’s three declarations.

chapters.n: They persist with loud, relentless shouts demanding crucifixion, and their voices win.

f.g: Insistent, pressing urgently.
Won out.

chapters.n: Pilate gives in and sentences Jesus as they demand. Political pressure overrides justice.

f.g: Pronounced the official verdict.

chapters.n: He releases the rebel and murderer they asked for and hands Jesus over to their will. The guilty goes free; the innocent dies in his place — a picture of the Atonement.
On the way, soldiers seize Simon from Cyrene in North Africa, coming in from the countryside, and force him to carry the cross behind Jesus — a picture of discipleship.

f.g: From Cyrene, a city in modern Libya with a large Jewish community.

chapters.n: A large crowd follows, including women mourning and wailing for Him.

f.g: Beat their breasts and wailed in grief.

chapters.n: Jesus, even in His agony, turns to them: Daughters of Jerusalem, don’t weep for Me, but for yourselves and your children. His concern is for them.

f.g: Women of the city.

chapters.n: Days are coming when people will say childless women are fortunate — so terrible will be Jerusalem’s destruction.

f.g: Breasts that never nursed.

chapters.n: People will beg the mountains to fall on them and the hills to hide them — words from Hosea expressing utter despair.
A proverb: if they do this to green, living wood (the innocent Jesus), what will happen to dry wood (a guilty, ripened-for-judgment nation)?

f.g: Green wood burns poorly; dry wood burns readily.

chapters.n: Two criminals are led out with Him to be executed.

f.g: Criminals, evildoers.

chapters.n: At the place called the Skull, they crucify Him between the two criminals — numbered with transgressors, as Isaiah foretold.

f.g: From the Latin calvaria, “skull”; Aramaic Golgotha.

f.w: one on the right hand, and the other on the left

chapters.n: Jesus prays for His executioners: Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they’re doing. The JST clarifies He meant the soldiers. Meanwhile they gamble for His clothes.

f.g: JST Luke 23:35 adds: “Meaning the soldiers who crucified him.”
Threw dice or drew lots.

chapters.n: The people stand watching. The leaders sneer: He saved others — let Him save Himself if He’s really God’s Messiah. Ironically, He saves others precisely by not saving Himself.

f.g: Scoffed, sneered.

chapters.n: The soldiers mock Him too, offering Him sour wine.

f.g: Cheap sour wine, the common drink of soldiers.

chapters.n: They jeer: if You’re the King of the Jews, save Yourself.

f.g: The temptation to come down echoes Satan’s wilderness challenges.

chapters.n: A sign above Him reads “This is the King of the Jews” in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew. Meant as mockery, it proclaims the truth to the whole world.

f.g: An inscription naming a condemned person’s crime.
The languages of culture, government, and religion — understood by all present.

chapters.n: One of the criminals hanging beside Him joins the insults: If You’re the Christ, save Yourself and us!

f.g: Insulted, abused Him.

chapters.n: The other criminal rebukes him: don’t you fear God? You’re under the same sentence.

f.g: Sentence of punishment.

chapters.n: We deserve this, he says, but this man has done nothing wrong. Even a dying criminal testifies to Jesus’ innocence.

f.w: the due reward of our deeds
f.g: What our actions deserve.
Nothing wrong.

chapters.n: Then he speaks to Jesus: remember me when You come into Your kingdom. He sees a King in a dying man.

Jesus promises: today you will be with Me in paradise. Latter-day Saints understand paradise as part of the spirit world, where Jesus went to minister after His death — and where this man would hear the gospel.

f.g: A Persian word for a garden; here the world of spirits after death.

chapters.n: From about noon until three in the afternoon, darkness covers the whole land. In the Americas, three days of darkness marked His death.

f.g: About noon (counting from sunrise).

chapters.n: The sun stops shining, and the temple veil — the curtain before the Holy of Holies — tears in two. The way into God’s presence is opened through Christ.

f.w: the veil of the temple was rent

f.g: Torn.

chapters.n: Jesus cries out loudly and prays, quoting Psalm 31: Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit. Then He dies. He gives up His life willingly; no one takes it from Him.

f.w: Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit

f.g: Breathed His last; released His spirit.

chapters.n: The Roman centurion in charge praises God and says: surely this was a righteous man. A Gentile soldier confirms His innocence.

f.g: A Roman officer commanding about a hundred soldiers.
Matthew and Mark record him saying “the Son of God.”

chapters.n: The crowds who came to watch go home beating their chests in grief and regret.

f.g: A sign of sorrow and repentance.

chapters.n: His friends, including the women who followed Him from Galilee, watch from a distance. These faithful women will be key witnesses to the burial and the empty tomb.

f.w: the women that followed him from Galilee

chapters.n: A man named Joseph enters the story — a member of the council, good and righteous.

f.g: A member of the Sanhedrin.

chapters.n: He had not agreed with the council’s decision. From Arimathea, a Judean town, he was looking for God’s kingdom.

f.g: A town in Judea, perhaps the birthplace of Samuel (Ramathaim).

f.w: waited for the kingdom of God

chapters.n: He goes to Pilate and asks for Jesus’ body — a courageous act that publicly identified him with the condemned man.
He takes the body down, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a new tomb cut into rock, never before used — fulfilling Isaiah’s words about a rich man’s grave.

f.g: Tomb.

f.w: wherein never man before was laid

chapters.n: It is Preparation Day, Friday, and the Sabbath is about to begin at sundown. The burial must be rushed.

f.g: The day before the Sabbath, when everything was readied.
Was beginning.

chapters.n: The Galilean women follow and see the tomb and how His body was placed. They will know exactly where to return.

f.g: Their eyewitness of the burial makes their later witness of the empty tomb credible.

chapters.n: They go home and prepare spices and perfumed oils for His body, then rest on the Sabbath as the law commands — even in grief, obedient.

f.g: Aromatic spices and oils used to honor and anoint a body.

chapters.n: At dawn on Sunday, the first day of the week, the women return to the tomb with the spices they prepared, intending to finish anointing His body. Christians would come to worship on this day in honor of the Resurrection.

f.w: the first day of the week
f.g: Sunday — later called the Lord’s Day.

chapters.n: They find the large stone that sealed the entrance already rolled away.

f.g: Rolling-stone tombs were sealed with a heavy disc set in a groove.

chapters.n: Going inside, they find no body. Luke calls Him “the Lord Jesus” — a title of His risen glory.

f.g: This full title first appears in Luke here, after the Resurrection.

chapters.n: As they stand puzzled, two men in dazzling clothing appear beside them. Verse 23 calls them angels; the JST describes them as angels as well.

f.g: Clothing gleaming like lightning — a sign of heavenly beings.
At a loss, confused.

chapters.n: Terrified, the women bow to the ground. The angels ask: why are you looking for the living among the dead?

f.w: Why seek ye the living among the dead?

chapters.n: He isn’t here — He has risen! Remember what He told you back in Galilee.

f.w: He is not here, but is risen

chapters.n: He said the Son of Man must be handed over to sinners, crucified, and rise on the third day. Everything happened just as He foretold.
Then they remember His words. Remembering is often the beginning of understanding.
They leave the tomb and report everything to the eleven apostles and the other disciples. These women are the first witnesses of the Resurrection.

f.g: The Twelve minus Judas.

chapters.n: Luke names them: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and other women. Women who supported Jesus in Galilee now carry the greatest news in history.
The apostles think it’s nonsense and don’t believe them. Even those closest to Jesus struggled to accept the Resurrection at first.

f.g: Nonsense, delirious talk — a word used by physicians for the ravings of the sick.

chapters.n: Peter, though, gets up and runs to the tomb. Stooping to look in, he sees only the linen grave cloths lying there and leaves amazed, wondering what has happened.

f.w: the linen clothes laid by themselves
f.g: The burial wrappings left behind — no thief would have unwrapped a body.

chapters.n: That same day, two disciples walk to Emmaus, a village about seven miles from Jerusalem.

f.g: Sixty stadia — about seven miles (11 km).
Its exact location is uncertain today.

chapters.n: They discuss everything that has happened.

f.g: The trial, crucifixion, and the strange reports of the empty tomb.

chapters.n: As they talk and debate, Jesus Himself comes up and walks with them.

f.g: Talked and discussed back and forth.

chapters.n: But they are kept from recognizing Him. God allowed them to learn from the scriptures before they saw Him with their eyes.

f.g: Held back, restrained.

chapters.n: He asks what they are discussing so intently as they walk along, looking so sad.

f.g: What kind of words.

chapters.n: Cleopas replies: are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who hasn’t heard what happened there these past days? The irony is rich — he is speaking to the one person who knows best.

f.g: Possibly the same as Clopas in John 19:25.
A visitor or pilgrim.

chapters.n: Jesus asks, “What things?” They tell Him about Jesus of Nazareth, a prophet powerful in action and word before God and all the people.

f.w: a prophet mighty in deed and word

chapters.n: They explain how their own leaders handed Him over to be condemned and crucified.

f.g: Handed Him over.

chapters.n: “We had hoped He was the one who would redeem Israel.” Their hope is in the past tense. And now it’s the third day since these things happened.

f.g: We had hoped.
Many expected the Messiah to free Israel from Rome.

chapters.n: Some women from their group have amazed them — they went to the tomb early this morning...

f.g: Amazed, bewildered.

chapters.n: ...and didn’t find His body. They came back saying they had seen angels who said He is alive.
Some went to check and found the tomb exactly as the women said — but they didn’t see Him.

f.g: The empty tomb alone did not yet produce faith.

chapters.n: Jesus responds: how foolish and slow you are to believe everything the prophets said!

f.g: Here “thoughtless, without understanding” — a gentle rebuke, not an insult.

chapters.n: Wasn’t it necessary for the Messiah to suffer these things and then enter His glory? The cross was not a defeat but the path to glory.

f.w: Ought not Christ to have suffered

chapters.n: Starting with Moses and all the prophets, He explains everything the scriptures say about Him. The whole Old Testament testifies of Christ.

f.g: Explained in detail.

chapters.n: Approaching their village, Jesus acts as though He will keep going. He waits to be invited.

f.w: he made as though he would have gone further

chapters.n: They urge Him strongly to stay with them, since it’s nearly evening. He goes in to stay.

f.g: Urged strongly.
Stay with us.

chapters.n: At the table, He takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them — the same actions as at the feeding of the five thousand and the Last Supper.

f.w: took bread, and blessed it, and brake

chapters.n: Their eyes are opened and they recognize Him — and then He vanishes from their sight.
They say to each other: weren’t our hearts burning inside us as He talked with us and opened the scriptures? The burning was the witness of the Spirit.

f.w: Did not our heart burn within us

chapters.n: At once — despite the hour and the seven-mile walk — they hurry back to Jerusalem and find the Eleven and others gathered.

f.g: Immediately; their joy couldn’t wait until morning.

chapters.n: Before they can speak, the group tells them: the Lord has really risen and has appeared to Simon Peter!
The two share their story of the road and how they recognized Him in the breaking of bread.

f.g: A phrase that came to describe the sacrament in the early Church.

chapters.n: While they are still talking, Jesus Himself stands among them and says, “Peace be with you.”
They are startled and frightened, thinking they are seeing a ghost.

f.g: A ghost, a disembodied spirit.

chapters.n: He asks why they are troubled and why doubts are rising in their hearts.

f.g: Doubts, questioning thoughts.

chapters.n: Look at My hands and feet — it’s really Me. Touch Me and see: a spirit doesn’t have flesh and bones as I do. This is a central witness of a literal, physical resurrection.

f.w: a spirit hath not flesh and bones

chapters.n: He shows them His hands and feet, still bearing the wounds of the nails.
They are so overjoyed and amazed they can hardly believe it. He asks: do you have anything to eat?

f.g: It seemed too good to be true.
Food.

chapters.n: They give Him a piece of broiled fish and some honeycomb.

f.g: Grilled fish, a common Galilean food.

chapters.n: He eats it in front of them — proof that His resurrected body is real and tangible.
He reminds them of His teaching: everything written about Him in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms must be fulfilled. These were the three divisions of the Hebrew scriptures.

f.w: the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms
f.g: The three sections of the Jewish scriptures: Law, Prophets, and Writings (headed by Psalms).

chapters.n: He opens their minds to understand the scriptures — the same gift He gave on the Emmaus road.
This is what was written: the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day.

f.g: Was necessary for, was fitting for.

f.w: rise from the dead the third day

chapters.n: And repentance and forgiveness of sins must be preached in His name to all nations, starting in Jerusalem. This is the mission that Luke’s second book, Acts, describes.

f.g: Forgiveness, release from sins.

f.w: among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem

chapters.n: You are witnesses of these things. The apostles are called above all to testify of the risen Christ.
He will send what the Father promised — the Holy Ghost. They must wait in Jerusalem until clothed with power from on high, fulfilled on the day of Pentecost.

f.g: Clothed, endowed.

chapters.n: He leads them out to the area of Bethany on the Mount of Olives, raises His hands, and blesses them.

f.w: lifted up his hands, and blessed them

chapters.n: While blessing them, He is parted from them and taken up into heaven. His final act on earth recorded by Luke is a blessing.
They worship Him and return to Jerusalem filled with joy — not sorrow. They know He lives and will return.

f.g: They now recognize Him as divine.

chapters.n: They are constantly at the temple praising God. Luke’s Gospel begins and ends in the temple, bookending the story of God’s salvation in Christ.
